title: VIII. The Scandalous Scene
paragraphs: Miüsov, being a man of breeding and refinement, couldn't help feeling a twinge of shame as he and Ivan walked over to the Father Superior's: he was embarrassed at having lost his temper. He felt he should have been too far above that contemptible wretch Fyodor Pavlovitch to let him upset him in Father Zossima's cell, and so to lose his composure. "The monks weren't to blame, in any case," he thought, on the steps. "And if the people here are decent -- and I gather the Father Superior is a gentleman -- why not be friendly and courteous with them? I won't argue, I'll go along with everything, I'll win them over with politeness, and... and... show them I have nothing to do with that Aesop, that clown, that Pierrot, and that I've simply been dragged into this business the same as they have."

He resolved to drop his lawsuit against the monastery and give up his claims to the timber and fishing rights on the spot. He was all the more willing to do this because the rights had become worth much less, and in any case he had only the vaguest notion where the wood and the river in question even were.

These excellent resolutions were only reinforced when he stepped into the Father Superior's dining room -- though strictly speaking it wasn't a dining room, since the Father Superior had only two rooms in all; they were, however, considerably larger and more comfortable than Father Zossima's. Still, there was nothing very luxurious about how these rooms were furnished either. The furniture was mahogany upholstered in leather, in the old style of 1820; the floor wasn't even stained, though everything gleamed with cleanliness, and there were fine flowers in abundance on the windowsills. The most sumptuous thing in the room just then, of course, was the beautifully laid table. The cloth was spotless, the service gleamed; there were three kinds of freshly baked bread, two bottles of wine, two of excellent mead, and a big glass jug of kvas -- the last two brewed at the monastery and famous throughout the district. There was no vodka. Rakitin reported afterward that there were five courses: sterlet soup with little fish pies, then boiled fish prepared in a special way, then salmon cutlets, ice pudding and stewed fruit, and finally blancmange. Rakitin had found all this out because he couldn't resist peeking into the kitchen, where he already had connections. He had connections everywhere, and got wind of everything. He had an anxious, envious temperament. He was well aware of his own considerable talents and, with characteristic vanity, exaggerated them further. He knew he was destined to play some prominent role, but Alyosha, who was fond of him, was troubled to see that his friend Rakitin was dishonorable and entirely unaware of being so, considering himself, on the contrary, a man of the highest integrity simply because he wouldn't pocket money left lying on a table. Neither Alyosha nor anyone else could have talked him out of that.

Rakitin, of course, was far too minor a figure to be invited to the dinner, to which Father Iosif, Father Païssy, and one other monk were the only residents of the monastery asked. They were already waiting when Miüsov, Kalganov, and Ivan arrived. The other guest, Maximov, stood a little apart, also waiting. The Father Superior stepped into the middle of the room to receive his guests. He was a tall, thin, yet still vigorous old man, his black hair streaked with gray, with a long, grave, ascetic face. He bowed to his guests in silence. This time, though, they came forward for his blessing. Miüsov even tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior drew it back in time to avoid the gesture. Ivan and Kalganov, however, went through the whole ceremony in the simplest and most complete way, kissing his hand as peasants do.

"We really must apologize most humbly, Your Reverence," Miüsov began, smiling ingratiatingly and speaking in a dignified, respectful tone. "Forgive us for coming without the gentleman you invited, Fyodor Pavlovitch. He felt he had to decline the honor of your hospitality, and not without reason. In the reverend Father Zossima's cell he was carried away by the unfortunate quarrel with his son and let slip words that were entirely out of place -- in fact, quite improper -- as" -- he glanced at the monks -- "Your Reverence is, no doubt, already aware. And so, recognizing that he was to blame, he felt genuine regret and shame, and asked me, along with his son Ivan Fyodorovitch, to convey his apologies and his regret to you. In short, he hopes and intends to make amends later. He asks your blessing, and begs you to forget what took place."

As he uttered the last word of this little speech, Miüsov fully recovered his self-satisfaction, and every trace of his earlier irritation vanished. He was once again in sincere and complete love with humanity.
The Father Superior listened to him with dignity, and, with a slight bow of the head, replied:
"I sincerely regret his absence. Perhaps at our table he might have come to like us, and we him. Please be seated, gentlemen."
He stood before the icon and began to say grace aloud. All bowed their heads reverently, and Maximov clasped his hands before him with particular fervor.

It was at this moment that Fyodor Pavlovitch pulled off his last prank. It should be noted that he really had meant to go home, and really had felt it was impossible to go and dine with the Father Superior as though nothing had happened, after his disgraceful behavior in the elder's cell. Not that he was terribly ashamed of himself -- quite the opposite, if anything. Still, he sensed it would be improper to go to dinner. But his creaking carriage had barely pulled up to the steps of the hotel, and he had barely climbed in, when he suddenly stopped short. He remembered his own words at the elder's: "I always feel, whenever I meet people, that I'm lower than everyone, and that they all take me for a buffoon; so let me play the buffoon, then, since every one of you is stupider and lower than I am." He was seized with a longing to get his revenge on everyone for his own bad behavior. He suddenly recalled being asked once, in the past, "Why do you hate so-and-so so much?" And he'd answered, with his shameless impudence, "I'll tell you why. He's never done me any harm. But I once played a dirty trick on him, and I've hated him ever since."

Remembering that now, he smiled quietly and maliciously, hesitating for a moment. His eyes gleamed, his lips actually trembled. "Well, since I've begun, I might as well go on," he decided. His dominant feeling at that moment might be summed up like this: "There's no rehabilitating myself now. So let me shame them for all I'm worth. I'll show them I don't care what they think -- that's all there is to it!"

He told the coachman to wait, and with quick steps went back to the monastery, straight to the Father Superior's. He had no clear idea what he meant to do, but he knew he couldn't restrain himself, and that the smallest push might drive him to the utmost extremes of shamelessness -- but only shamelessness, nothing criminal, nothing he could be legally punished for. When it came down to it, he could always hold himself back, and had in fact sometimes marveled at himself on that score. He appeared in the Father Superior's dining room just as the prayer was ending and everyone was moving toward the table. Standing in the doorway, he surveyed the company, and, laughing his long, insolent, malicious chuckle, looked every one of them boldly in the face. "They thought I'd gone, and here I am again!" he called out to the whole room.

For one moment everyone stared at him without a word; and at once everyone sensed that something revolting, grotesque, downright scandalous was about to happen. Miüsov's mood swung instantly from the most benevolent to the most savage. Every feeling that had settled and died down in his heart flared up again at once.
"No! This I cannot bear!" he cried. "I absolutely cannot -- and... I certainly cannot!"
The blood rushed to his head. He actually stammered; but he was past caring about style, and he snatched up his hat.
"What is it he can't bear?" cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. "What is it he absolutely cannot and certainly cannot? Your Reverence, am I to come in or not? Will you have me as your guest?"

"You are welcome with all my heart," the Superior answered. "Gentlemen," he added, "I earnestly beg you to set aside your differences, and to be united in love and family harmony -- with prayer to the Lord at our humble table."
"No, no, it's impossible!" cried Miüsov, beside himself.

"Well, if it's impossible for Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it's impossible for me too, and I won't stay. That's why I came. I'll stick with Pyotr Alexandrovitch wherever he goes now. If you leave, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I'll leave too; if you stay, I'll stay. You stung him, Father Superior, talking about family harmony -- he won't even admit he's my relation. Isn't that right, von Sohn? Here's von Sohn. How are you, von Sohn?"
"Are you talking to me?" Maximov muttered, puzzled.
"Of course I'm talking to you," cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. "Who else? The Father Superior can hardly be von Sohn."
"But I'm not von Sohn either. I'm Maximov."

"No, you're von Sohn. Your Reverence, do you know who von Sohn was? It was a famous murder case. He was killed in a house of ill repute -- I believe that's what such places are called among you people -- killed and robbed, and, in spite of his venerable age, nailed up in a crate and shipped from Petersburg to Moscow in the luggage car, while the whores who nailed him up sang songs and played the harp -- or rather, the piano. So this is that very same von Sohn. Risen from the dead, hasn't he, von Sohn?"
"What's going on? What is this?" voices came from among the monks.
"Let's go," cried Miüsov, turning to Kalganov.

"No, excuse me," Fyodor Pavlovitch broke in shrilly, taking another step into the room. "Let me finish. Back there in the cell you scolded me for being disrespectful, just because I mentioned eating gudgeon, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. My relation Miüsov prefers to have more nobility than sincerity in his words, but I prefer more sincerity than nobility in mine -- and to hell with nobility! Isn't that right, von Sohn? Allow me, Father Superior -- though I'm a buffoon and I play the buffoon, still, I'm the soul of honor, and I want to speak my mind. Yes, I'm the soul of honor, while in Pyotr Alexandrovitch there's nothing but wounded vanity. I came here, perhaps, to take a look and speak my mind. My son Alexey is here, being saved. I'm his father; I care about his welfare, and it's my duty to care. While I've been playing the fool, I've been listening, and quietly watching everything; and now I want to give you the last act of the show. You know how things go with us? As a thing falls, so it lies. Once fallen, it must lie there forever. Not a bit of it! I intend to get up again. Holy Father, I'm indignant with you. Confession is a great sacrament, before which I'm ready to bow down in reverence; but back there in the cell they all kneel and confess out loud. Can it possibly be right to confess aloud? The holy Fathers ordained that confession be made in secret: only then does your confession remain a mystery, as it was in ancient times. But how can I explain to you, in front of everyone, that I did this and that -- well, you understand what I mean -- sometimes it wouldn't be proper to talk about it -- so it really is a scandal! No, Fathers, one could be carried along right into the arms of the Flagellants with you, I daresay... At the first opportunity I shall write to the Synod, and I shall take my son Alexey home."

We should note here that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew exactly where to find the weak spot. There had once been malicious rumors, which had even reached the Archbishop -- not only about our monastery, but about others where the institution of elders existed -- that the elders were shown too much respect, to the detriment of the Superior's authority, and that they abused the sacrament of confession, and so on and so forth -- absurd charges that had long since died away of their own accord everywhere. But the spirit of folly that had seized Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was carrying him on the current of his own nerves down into ever lower depths of disgrace, prompted him to dredge up this old slander. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't understand a word of it, and couldn't even explain it sensibly, since on this occasion no one had been kneeling and confessing aloud in the elder's cell at all, so he couldn't possibly have seen anything of the kind. He was speaking only from a confused memory of old gossip. But the moment he'd finished his foolish tirade, he felt he'd been talking absolute nonsense, and immediately longed to prove to his audience, and above all to himself, that he hadn't been talking nonsense. And though he knew perfectly well that with every word he'd be adding more and more absurdity, he couldn't stop himself, and plunged blindly on.
"How disgraceful!" cried Pyotr Alexandrovitch.

"Forgive me!" said the Father Superior. "It was written long ago: 'Many have begun to speak against me, and have uttered evil sayings about me. And hearing it, I have said to myself: it is the correction of the Lord, and He has sent it to heal my vain soul.' And so we thank you humbly, honored guest!" And he made Fyodor Pavlovitch a low bow.

"Tut, tut, tut -- sanctimony and stock phrases! Old phrases, old gestures. Old lies and formal genuflections. We know all about them. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, just like Schiller's Robbers. I don't like falsehood, Fathers, I want the truth. But the truth isn't found in eating gudgeon, and that I proclaim out loud! Monk fathers, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for it? Why, for a reward like that, I'll come and fast too! No, holy monk, try being virtuous out in the world, do some good for society, without shutting yourself up in a monastery at other people's expense, and without expecting a reward up above for it -- you'll find that a good deal harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?" He went up to the table. "Old port wine, mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. For shame, for shame, fathers! That's a step up from gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have brought out -- he he he! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the laborer, bringing here the farthing earned by his calloused hand, wrung out of his family and the tax collector! You're bleeding the people, you know, holy fathers."
"This is simply disgraceful!" said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy kept stubbornly silent. Miüsov rushed out of the room, and Kalganov after him.

"Well, Father, I'll follow Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I won't come to see you again. You could beg me on your knees and I still wouldn't come. I sent you a thousand roubles, and now you've started keeping an eye on me. He he he! No, I'll say no more. I'm taking my revenge for my youth, for all the humiliation I endured." He thumped the table with his fist in a fit of feigned emotion. "This monastery has played a huge part in my life! It's cost me many bitter tears. You used to turn my wife, the crazy one, against me. You cursed me with bell and book, you spread stories about me all over the place. Enough, fathers! This is the age of Liberalism, the age of steamships and railways. You won't get a thousand out of me, nor a hundred roubles, nor a hundred farthings!"

We should note again that our monastery had never played any great part in his life, and he had never shed a single bitter tear on its account. But he was so carried away by his own performance of emotion that for one moment he very nearly believed it himself. He was so moved he was almost weeping. But at that very instant he sensed it was time to pull back.
The Father Superior bowed his head at this malicious lie, and once more spoke with feeling:
"It is written again: 'Bear patiently and gladly the dishonor that comes upon you through no fault of your own; be not troubled, and do not hate the one who has dishonored you.' And so shall we."

"Tut, tut, tut! Bethinking yourself, and the rest of the rigmarole. Think what you like, Fathers, I'm going. But I'll take my son Alexey away from here for good, by my parental authority. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my most dutiful son, permit me to order you to follow me. Von Sohn, what are you staying here for? Come and visit me in town. There's fun to be had there. It's only a short verst away; instead of lenten oil, I'll give you suckling pig and buckwheat. We'll have dinner with brandy and liqueur to go with it... I've got cloudberry wine. Hey, von Sohn, don't miss your chance." And he strode out, shouting and gesturing.
It was at that moment that Rakitin caught sight of him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
"Alexey!" his father shouted from a distance, catching sight of him. "You come home to me today, for good, and bring your pillow and mattress with you, and leave no trace behind."

Alyosha stood rooted to the spot, watching the scene in silence. Meanwhile Fyodor Pavlovitch had climbed into the carriage, and Ivan was about to follow him in grim silence, without even turning to say goodbye to Alyosha. But at this point another almost unbelievable scene of grotesque buffoonery put the finishing touch on the whole episode. Maximov suddenly appeared beside the carriage. He came running up, panting, afraid of being too late. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him running. He was in such a hurry that he set his foot right on the step where Ivan's left foot still rested, and, clutching at the carriage, kept trying to jump in. "I'm coming with you!" he kept shouting, laughing a thin, delighted laugh, a look of reckless glee on his face. "Take me too!"

"There!" cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted. "Didn't I say he was von Sohn? It's von Sohn himself, risen from the dead. Why, how did you break free? What kind of von-Sohn business were you up to there? And how did you get away from the dinner? You must be a brazen fellow! I'm one myself, but I'm amazed at you, brother! Jump in, jump in! Let him through, Ivan. It'll be fun. He can lie down somewhere at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or perch up on the box with the coachman. Hop up onto the box, von Sohn!"
But Ivan, who had by now taken his seat, without a word gave Maximov a violent punch in the chest and sent him flying. It was pure chance he didn't fall.
"Drive on!" Ivan shouted angrily at the coachman.
"What are you doing, what's got into you? Why did you do that?" Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage had already driven off. Ivan made no reply.
"Well, you're a piece of work," Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.
After a pause of two minutes, glancing sideways at his son: "Why, it was you who got up this whole business at the monastery. You urged it on, you approved of it. So why are you angry now?"
"You've talked enough rubbish. You might rest a bit now," Ivan snapped sullenly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch fell silent again for two minutes.
"A drop of brandy would be nice right now," he observed sententiously, but Ivan made no response.
"You'll have some too, when we get home."
Ivan said nothing.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
"But I'll take Alyosha away from the monastery all the same, much as you'll dislike it, my most honored Karl von Moor."
Ivan shrugged his shoulders contemptuously, and turning away, stared out at the road. And they didn't exchange another word the whole way home.

title: I. In The Servants’ Quarters
paragraphs: The Karamazovs' house was nowhere near the center of town, but it wasn't quite on the outskirts either. It was a pleasant old two-story house, painted gray, with a red iron roof. It was roomy and cozy, and looked like it could last many more years yet. There were all sorts of unexpected little cupboards and closets and staircases tucked away in it. It had rats, but Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't much mind them. "One doesn't feel quite so alone in the evening when one's left by oneself," he used to say. It was his habit to send the servants off to the lodge for the night and lock himself up alone in the house. The lodge was a roomy, solid building in the yard. Fyodor Pavlovitch had the cooking done there, even though there was a kitchen in the house; he didn't like the smell of cooking, and, winter and summer alike, the dishes were carried across the courtyard to him. The house had been built for a large family; there was room for five times as many people, servants included. But at the time of our story no one lived in the house except Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan. And in the lodge there were only three servants: old Grigory, his old wife Marfa, and a young man named Smerdyakov. A few words are in order about these three. We've already said something about old Grigory. He was firm and stubborn, and pursued his goal blindly and obstinately once he'd been brought, by some reasoning or other -- often quite illogical -- to believe it was unquestionably right. He was honest and incorruptible. His wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, had obeyed her husband's will without question her whole life, and yet she had pestered him relentlessly after the emancipation of the serfs. She was set on leaving Fyodor Pavlovitch and opening a little shop in Moscow with their small savings. But Grigory settled it once and for all: "the woman's talking nonsense, since every woman is dishonest," and they shouldn't abandon their old master, whatever he might be, because "that was now their duty."
"Do you understand what duty is?" he asked Marfa Ignatyevna.
"I understand what duty means, Grigory Vassilyevitch, but why it's our duty to stay here I'll never understand," Marfa answered firmly.
"Well, then don't understand it. But that's how it will be. And you hold your tongue."

And so it was. They didn't leave, and Fyodor Pavlovitch promised them a small wage, and paid it regularly. Grigory also knew he had an undeniable hold over his master. That was true, and he was well aware of it. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a stubborn, cunning buffoon, and yet, though his will was strong enough "in some of life's affairs," as he put it, he found himself, to his own surprise, extremely feeble in the face of certain other emergencies. He knew his weaknesses, and was afraid of them. There are situations in which a man has to keep a sharp lookout, and that isn't easy without someone trustworthy at hand, and Grigory was the most trustworthy of men. Fyodor Pavlovitch had, many times over the course of his life, narrowly escaped a sound thrashing thanks to Grigory's intervention, and each time the old servant gave him a good talking-to besides. But it wasn't only thrashings that Fyodor Pavlovitch was afraid of. There were graver occasions, subtler and more complicated ones, when Fyodor Pavlovitch couldn't have explained the extraordinary craving that sometimes came over him, quite without warning, for someone loyal and devoted. It was almost a sickness. Corrupt, and often cruel in his lust, like some noxious insect, Fyodor Pavlovitch was sometimes, when drunk, overcome by a superstitious terror and a moral convulsion that took on an almost physical form. "My soul's fairly quaking in my throat at those times," he used to say. At such moments he liked to know there was, somewhere close by -- in the lodge, if not in the room itself -- a strong, faithful man, virtuous and unlike himself, who had witnessed all his debauchery and knew all his secrets, but who, out of sheer devotion, was ready to overlook all of it, not to oppose him, and above all not to reproach him or threaten him with anything, in this world or the next, and, if it came to it, to defend him -- from whom? From someone unknown, but terrible and dangerous. What he needed was to feel that there was another man there, an old and tested friend, whom he could summon in his darkest moments just to look at his face, or perhaps exchange a few entirely trivial words with him. And if the old servant wasn't angry, he felt comforted; if he was angry, he felt more dejected still. It even happened, though rarely, that Fyodor Pavlovitch would go out to the lodge at night to wake Grigory and fetch him for a moment. When the old man came, Fyodor Pavlovitch would start talking about the most trivial matters, and would soon let him go again, sometimes even with a joke. And once he'd gone, Fyodor Pavlovitch would climb into bed with a curse and sleep the sleep of the righteous. Something of the same sort had happened to Fyodor Pavlovitch when Alyosha arrived. Alyosha had "pierced his heart" by "living with him, seeing everything, and blaming nothing." What's more, Alyosha had brought with him something his father had never known before: a complete absence of contempt for him, and an unwavering kindness, a perfectly natural, unaffected devotion to the old man, who deserved it so little. All this came as a complete surprise to the old profligate, who had cut himself off from every family tie. It was a new and astonishing experience for him, a man who until then had loved nothing but "evil." When Alyosha left him, he admitted to himself that he had learned something he'd never before been willing to learn.

I've already mentioned that Grigory had detested Adelaida Ivanovna, Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife and Dmitri's mother, and that, by contrast, he had defended Sofya Ivanovna, the poor "crazy woman," against his master and against anyone who dared speak ill or lightly of her. His sympathy for the unhappy wife had become something sacred to him, so that even now, twenty years on, he couldn't bear a disparaging word about her from anyone, and would immediately check the offender. Outwardly, Grigory was cold, dignified, and taciturn, and spoke, weighing his words, without a trace of frivolity. It was impossible to tell, at first glance, whether he loved his meek, obedient wife; but he really did love her, and she knew it.

Marfa Ignatyevna was by no means unintelligent; she was, in fact, probably shrewder than her husband, or at least more sensible than he was in practical matters, and yet she had deferred to him in everything without question or complaint ever since their marriage, and respected him for his spiritual superiority. It was remarkable how little they spoke to one another over the course of their lives, and then only about the most necessary daily matters. The grave, dignified Grigory turned over all his worries and duties alone in his own mind, so that Marfa Ignatyevna had long since grown used to the fact that he didn't need her advice. She felt that her husband respected her silence, and took it as a sign of her good sense. He had struck her only once in his life, and even then only lightly. Once, during the year after Fyodor Pavlovitch's marriage to Adelaida Ivanovna, the village girls and women -- serfs, at that time -- were gathered before the house to sing and dance. They were just beginning "In the Green Meadows" when Marfa, then a young woman, stepped forward and danced "the Russian dance" -- not in the village fashion, but as she'd danced it while in service in the household of the wealthy Miüsov family, in their private theater, where the actors had been taught to dance by a dancing master brought from Moscow. Grigory saw how his wife danced, and, an hour later, at home in their cottage, gave her a lesson, pulling her hair a little. But that was the end of it: the beating was never repeated, and Marfa Ignatyevna gave up dancing.

God hadn't blessed them with children. One child was born, but it died. Grigory was fond of children, and wasn't ashamed to show it. When Adelaida Ivanovna ran off, Grigory took Dmitri, then a child of three, combed his hair and washed him in a tub with his own hands, and looked after him for nearly a year. Afterward he looked after Ivan and Alyosha too, for which the general's widow rewarded him with a slap in the face; but all that has already been told. The only happiness his own child ever brought him came in the months of waiting for its birth. When it was born, he was overwhelmed with grief and horror. The baby had six fingers. Grigory was so crushed by this that he not only fell silent until the day of the christening, but kept away in the garden entirely. It was spring, and he spent three days digging in the kitchen garden. The christening was set for the third day; by then Grigory had come to a decision. Going into the cottage where the clergy had gathered and the guests had arrived, Fyodor Pavlovitch among them, who was to stand godfather, he suddenly announced that the baby "shouldn't be christened at all." He said this quietly, briefly, forcing the words out, staring dully and fixedly at the priest.
"Why not?" the priest asked, with good-humored surprise.
"Because it's a dragon," Grigory muttered.
"A dragon? What dragon?"
Grigory said nothing for a while. "It's a confusion of nature," he muttered vaguely, but firmly, clearly unwilling to say any more.

They laughed, and of course the poor baby was christened. Grigory prayed earnestly at the font, but his opinion of the newborn remained unchanged. Even so, he didn't interfere in any way. As long as the sickly infant lived, he hardly looked at it, tried in fact not to notice it, and for the most part stayed out of the cottage. But when, after two weeks, the baby died of thrush, he laid the child in its little coffin himself, looked at it in profound grief, and, when they were filling in the shallow little grave, fell to his knees and bowed down to the earth. For years afterward he never mentioned his child, and Marfa never spoke of the baby in front of him, and even when Grigory wasn't present she never spoke of it above a whisper. Marfa noticed that, from the day of the burial, he devoted himself to "religion," and took up reading the Lives of the Saints, mostly sitting alone in silence, always with his big, round, silver-rimmed spectacles on. He rarely read aloud, only perhaps during Lent. He was fond of the Book of Job, and had somehow gotten hold of a copy of the sayings and sermons of "the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian," which he read over and over for years, understanding very little of it, but perhaps prizing and loving it all the more for that. Lately he had begun listening to the teachings of the Flagellant sect settled in the area. He was evidently shaken by them, but judged it improper to go over to the new faith. His habit of theological reading gave him an air of even greater gravity.

He was perhaps predisposed to mysticism. And the birth of his deformed child, and its death, had, as though by some special design, been accompanied by another strange and marvelous event which, as he said later, had left a "stamp" on his soul. It so happened that, on the very night after his child's burial, Marfa was woken by the wail of a newborn baby. She was frightened and woke her husband. He listened and said he thought it sounded more like someone groaning -- "might be a woman." He got up and dressed. It was a fairly warm night in May. Going down the steps, he distinctly heard groans coming from the garden. But the gate from the yard into the garden was locked at night, and there was no other way in, since it was enclosed all around by a strong, high fence. Going back into the house, Grigory lit a lantern, took the garden key, and, paying no attention to his wife's hysterical fears -- she was still convinced she'd heard a child crying, her own baby, calling for her -- went into the garden in silence. There he heard at once that the groans were coming from the bathhouse near the garden gate, and that they were a woman's groans. Opening the bathhouse door, he saw a sight that froze him where he stood. An idiot girl who wandered the streets, known to the whole town by the nickname Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (Stinking Lizaveta), had gotten into the bathhouse and had just given birth to a child. She lay dying, the baby beside her. She said nothing, for she had never been able to speak. But her story deserves a chapter of its own.

title: II. Lizaveta
paragraphs: There was one detail that struck Grigory in particular, and confirmed a very unpleasant, repellent suspicion. This Lizaveta was a tiny, dwarfish creature, "not five feet if you spared her an inch," as many of the devout old women said of her, pityingly, after her death. Her broad, healthy, red face had a look of blank idiocy, and the fixed stare in her eyes was unpleasant, despite their meek expression. She wandered about, summer and winter alike, barefoot, wearing nothing but a hempen shift. Her coarse, almost black hair curled like lamb's wool, forming a sort of huge cap on her head. It was always caked with mud, with leaves, twigs, and shavings clinging to it, since she always slept on the ground, in the dirt. Her father, a homeless, sickly drunkard named Ilya, had lost everything and spent years working for various well-to-do tradespeople. Her mother had died long before. Vicious and diseased, Ilya used to beat Lizaveta savagely whenever she came back to him. But she rarely did, since everyone in town was ready to look after her, as an idiot and thus especially dear to God. Ilya's employers, and plenty of others in town, especially among the tradespeople, tried to dress her better, and always rigged her out with tall boots and a sheepskin coat for the winter. But although she let them dress her up without resisting, she would usually wander off, most often to the cathedral porch, and take off everything she'd been given -- kerchief, sheepskin, skirt, or boots -- leave it all there, and walk away barefoot in her shift as before. Once it happened that a new provincial governor, making a tour of inspection through our town, saw Lizaveta and was wounded in his most delicate sensibilities. And although he was told she was an idiot, he declared that for a young woman of twenty to wander about in nothing but a shift was a breach of propriety, and must not happen again. But the governor went his way, and Lizaveta was left as she was. At last her father died, which made her all the more acceptable in the eyes of the town's religious people, as an orphan. In fact, everyone seemed to like her; even the boys didn't tease her, and the boys of our town, the schoolboys especially, are a mischievous lot. She would walk into strange houses, and no one drove her away. Everyone was kind to her and gave her something. If given a copper, she'd take it and drop it at once into the alms box at the church or the prison. If given a roll or a bun at the market, she'd hand it to the first child she met. Sometimes she'd stop one of the wealthiest ladies in town and give it to her, and the lady would be glad to take it. She herself never touched anything but black bread and water. If she went into an expensive shop where costly goods or money lay about, no one kept watch on her, for they knew that even if she saw thousands of roubles left unguarded, she wouldn't have touched a farthing of it. She hardly ever went to church. She slept either in the church porch or climbed over a fence -- there are still many fences instead of hedges in our town to this day -- into someone's kitchen garden. At least once a week she'd turn up "at home," meaning at the house of her father's former employers, and in winter she went there every night, sleeping either in the passage or the cowshed. People marveled that she could endure such a life, but she was used to it, and, tiny as she was, she had a sturdy constitution. Some of the townspeople claimed she did all this out of pride, but that's hardly believable. She could barely speak, and only now and then let out an inarticulate grunt. How could she have been proud?

It happened one clear, warm, moonlit night in September -- many years ago now -- that five or six drunken revelers were making their way home from the club at a very late hour, by our provincial standards. They took the "back way," which ran between the back gardens of the houses, fences on either side. This path leads out onto the bridge over the long, foul-smelling ditch we're in the habit of calling a river. Among the nettles and burdocks under one of the fences, our revelers came upon Lizaveta asleep. They stopped to look at her, laughing, and began jesting with unrestrained coarseness. It occurred to one young gentleman to pose the whimsical question of whether anyone could possibly regard such a creature as a woman, and so on... They all agreed, with lofty disgust, that it was out of the question. But Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was among them, sprang forward and declared it was by no means out of the question, that there was, in fact, a certain piquancy to it, and so on... True, at the time he was overplaying his role as buffoon. He liked to put himself forward and entertain the company, ostensibly as an equal, though in reality he stood on servile footing with them. This was just around the time he'd received news of his first wife's death in Petersburg, and, crepe on his hat, was drinking and carrying on so shamelessly that even the most reckless among us were shocked at the sight of him. The revelers, of course, laughed at this unexpected opinion, and one of them even dared him to act on it. The others rejected the idea even more emphatically, though still with the utmost hilarity, and at last they went on their way. Later, Fyodor Pavlovitch swore he'd gone off with them, and perhaps he did -- no one knows for certain, and no one ever did. But five or six months later, the whole town was talking, with real and sincere indignation, about Lizaveta's condition, and trying to find out who the wretch was who had wronged her. Then suddenly a terrible rumor swept the town that this wretch was none other than Fyodor Pavlovitch. Who set the rumor going? Of that drunken party, five had since left town, and the only one still among us was an elderly, much-respected civil councilor, the father of grown daughters, who could hardly have spread the tale even if there'd been any basis for it. But rumor pointed straight at Fyodor Pavlovitch, and kept pointing at him. Of course this was no great trouble to him: he wouldn't have bothered contradicting a pack of tradespeople. In those days he was proud, and wouldn't condescend to speak with anyone outside his own circle of officials and gentry, whom he entertained so lavishly.

At the time, Grigory stood up for his master vigorously. He provoked quarrels and arguments in his defense, and managed to bring some people around to his side. "It's the wench's own fault," he insisted, and named the culprit as Karp, a dangerous escaped convict whose name was well known among us, since he'd been hiding out in our town. This theory sounded plausible enough, since people remembered Karp had been in the area that autumn, and had robbed three people. But this affair, and all the talk surrounding it, did nothing to turn popular sympathy away from the poor idiot. She was looked after more carefully than ever. A well-to-do merchant's widow named Kondratyev arranged to take her into her house at the end of April, meaning to keep her indoors until after her confinement. They kept a constant watch over her, but despite all their vigilance, she slipped away on the very last day and made her way into Fyodor Pavlovitch's garden. How, in her condition, she managed to climb over that high, sturdy fence remained a mystery. Some claimed someone must have lifted her over; others hinted at something more uncanny. The most likely explanation is the simplest one -- that Lizaveta, so used to clambering over fences to sleep in gardens, had somehow managed to scale this one too, despite her condition, and had jumped down, hurting herself in the fall.

Grigory rushed to Marfa and sent her to Lizaveta, while he himself ran to fetch an old midwife who lived nearby. They saved the baby, but Lizaveta died at dawn. Grigory took the baby, brought it home, and, making his wife sit down, placed it in her lap. "A child of God -- an orphan is kin to everyone," he said, "and to us above all. This one has been sent to us by our own lost little one, who has come to us from the devil's son and a holy innocent. Nurse him, and weep no more."

So Marfa raised the child. He was christened Pavel, to which people wasted no time adding Fyodorovitch (son of Fyodor). Fyodor Pavlovitch raised no objection to any of this, and found it amusing, though he continued to deny his responsibility vigorously. The townspeople were pleased at his taking in the foundling. Later on, Fyodor Pavlovitch invented a surname for the child, calling him Smerdyakov, after his mother's nickname.

So this Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovitch's second servant, and was living in the lodge with Grigory and Marfa at the time our story begins. He worked as the cook. I ought to say something about this Smerdyakov, but I'm embarrassed to keep my readers' attention so long occupied with these lowly servants, and I'll go back to my story now, hoping to say more about Smerdyakov as it goes on.

title: III. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—In Verse
paragraphs: Alyosha stood irresolute for a while after hearing his father's order shouted at him from the carriage. But uneasy as he was, he didn't simply stand still. That wasn't his way. He went straight to the kitchen to find out what his father had been doing up above. Then he set off, hoping that on the way he'd find some answer to the doubt that was tormenting him. I should add at once that his father's shouted command to come home "with his mattress and pillow" didn't frighten him in the least. He understood perfectly well that these peremptory shouts were just "a flourish," meant for effect. It was the same as when a tradesman in our town, celebrating his name day with a party of friends, got angry at being refused more vodka and smashed up his own crockery and furniture, tore his own and his wife's clothes, and finally broke his windows -- all purely for effect. The next day, sober again, he naturally regretted the broken cups and saucers. Alyosha knew that his father would let him go back to the monastery the next day, possibly even that same evening. He was also fully convinced that his father might hurt anyone else, but wouldn't hurt him. Alyosha was certain that no one in the whole world would ever want to hurt him, and what's more, he knew no one could. This was, for him, an axiom, taken for granted without question, and he went on his way relying on it without hesitation.

But at that moment a different kind of anxiety was troubling him, and it bothered him all the more because he couldn't put it into words. It was his fear of a woman -- of Katerina Ivanovna, who had so urgently begged him, in the note Madame Hohlakov had handed him, to come and see her about something. This request, and the necessity of going, had at once stirred an uneasy feeling in his heart, and that feeling had grown more and more painful all morning, despite the scenes at the hermitage and at the Father Superior's. It wasn't that he was anxious because he didn't know what she'd want to talk about, or what he'd have to answer. And he wasn't afraid of her simply as a woman. Though he knew little of women, he'd spent his whole life, from early childhood until he entered the monastery, entirely among them. He was afraid of that particular woman, Katerina Ivanovna. He'd been afraid of her from the first time he ever saw her. He'd only seen her two or three times, and had only ever managed to exchange a few words with her. He thought of her as a beautiful, proud, imperious girl. It wasn't her beauty that unsettled him, but something else. And the vagueness of his apprehension only made the apprehension itself worse. The girl's aims, he knew, were the noblest imaginable. She was trying, out of pure generosity, to save his brother Dmitri, even though Dmitri had already treated her badly. And yet, though Alyosha recognized and did full justice to all these fine, generous feelings, a shiver ran down his spine the moment he came near her house.

He reflected that he wouldn't find Ivan there, close a friend of hers as he was, since Ivan was certainly with their father now. Dmitri he was even more certain not to find there, and he had a foreboding as to why. And so his conversation would be with her alone. He had a strong urge to run and see his brother Dmitri before that fateful meeting. Without showing him the letter, he could still talk to him about it. But Dmitri lived a long way off, and was sure to be away from home besides. Standing still for a minute, he reached a final decision. Crossing himself with a quick, practiced gesture, and smiling at once, he turned resolutely toward the house of his formidable lady.

He knew where her house was. Going by the High Street and then across the marketplace would be a long way around. Though our town is small, it's spread out, and the houses are far apart. Meanwhile his father was expecting him, and might not yet have forgotten his order. He could be unreasonable, so Alyosha had to hurry there and back. He decided, then, to take a shortcut by the back way, since he knew every inch of the ground. This meant skirting fences, climbing over hurdles, and cutting through other people's backyards, where everyone he met knew him and greeted him. This way he could reach the High Street in half the time.

He had to pass the garden next to his father's, belonging to a little tumbledown house with four windows. The owner of this house, as Alyosha knew, was a bedridden old woman who lived with her daughter, once a genteel maid in generals' households in Petersburg. She'd been home a year now, nursing her sick mother. She always dressed in fine clothes, even though she and her old mother had sunk into such poverty that they went every day to Fyodor Pavlovitch's kitchen for soup and bread, which Marfa gave them freely. Yet, though the young woman came for soup, she'd never sold off any of her dresses, and one of them even had a long train -- a fact Alyosha had learned from Rakitin, who always knew everything going on in town. He'd forgotten it the moment he heard it, but now, reaching the garden, he remembered the dress with the train, raised his head, which had been bowed in thought, and came upon something quite unexpected.

Over the fence in the garden, Dmitri, standing on something, was leaning forward, gesturing wildly, waving him over, clearly afraid to say a word for fear of being overheard. Alyosha ran up to the fence.
"It's a good thing you looked up. I was about to shout to you," Mitya said in a joyful, hurried whisper. "Climb in here, quick! How splendid that you've come! I was just thinking about you!"

Alyosha was delighted too, but he didn't know how to get over the fence. Mitya put his powerful hand under his elbow to help him jump. Hitching up his cassock, Alyosha vaulted the fence with the agility of a barelegged street urchin.
"Well done! Now come on," said Mitya in an enthusiastic whisper.
"Where?" whispered Alyosha, looking around him and finding himself in a deserted garden with no one nearby but themselves. The garden was small, but the house was at least fifty paces off.
"There's no one here. Why are you whispering?" asked Alyosha.

"Why am I whispering? Devil take it!" cried Dmitri at the top of his lungs. "You see what ridiculous tricks nature plays on a man. I'm here in secret, keeping watch. I'll explain it all later, but the moment I knew it was a secret, I started whispering like a fool, when there's no need at all. Let's go. Over there. Till then, keep quiet. I want to kiss you.
Glory to God in the world, Glory to God in me ...
I was just repeating that, sitting here, before you came."

The garden covered about three acres, planted with trees only along the fence on all four sides. There were apple trees, maples, limes, and birches. The middle of the garden was open grass, from which several hundredweight of hay was carried away each summer. The garden was let out for a few roubles a summer. There were also beds of raspberries, currants, and gooseberries along the sides; a vegetable patch had lately been planted near the house.

Dmitri led his brother to the most secluded corner of the garden. There, in a thicket of lime trees and old bushes of black currant, elder, snowball, and lilac, stood a tumbledown green summer house, blackened with age. Its walls were latticework, but there was still enough of a roof to give shelter. God knows when this summer house was built. There was a story that it had gone up some fifty years before, put there by a retired colonel named von Schmidt, who'd owned the house back then. It was all falling apart now, the floor rotting, the planks loose, the woodwork smelling musty. Inside stood a green wooden table fixed into the ground, ringed by green benches still sturdy enough to sit on. Alyosha had noticed at once his brother's excited state, and, stepping into the arbor, saw a half-empty bottle of brandy and a wineglass on the table.
"That's brandy," Mitya laughed. "I see the look on your face: 'He's drinking again!' Distrust the apparition.

Distrust the worthless, lying crowd,
And lay aside thy doubts.

I'm not drinking, I'm only 'indulging,' as that pig, your Rakitin, likes to say. He'll be a civil councilor one day, but he'll always be talking about 'indulging.' Sit down. I could take you in my arms, Alyosha, and hold you so tight I'd crush you, because in the whole world -- really, in re-al-i-ty -- (can you take that in?) I love no one but you!"
He spoke the last words in a kind of rapture.

"No one but you, and one 'jade' I've fallen in love with, to my ruin. But being in love isn't the same as loving. You can be in love with a woman and still hate her. Remember that! I can still talk lightly about it. Sit down here by the table, I'll sit beside you and look at you, and go on talking. You keep quiet, and I'll go on talking, because the time has come. But on second thought, you know, I'd better keep my voice down, because here -- here -- you never know what ears might be listening. I'll explain everything; as they say, 'the story continues.' Why have I been longing for you? Why have I been thirsting for you all these days, and especially just now? It's been five days since I dropped anchor here. Because you're the only one I can tell everything to; because I have to, because I need you, because tomorrow I'm falling from the clouds, because tomorrow life ends and begins. Have you ever felt, ever dreamed, of falling down a cliff into a pit? That's exactly how I'm falling now, only it's not a dream. And I'm not afraid -- don't you be afraid either. At least, I am afraid, but I enjoy it. It's not really enjoyment, though -- it's ecstasy. Damn it all, whatever it is! A strong spirit, a weak spirit, a womanish spirit -- whatever it is! Let's praise nature: look at that sunshine, how clear the sky is, the leaves all green, still summer; four in the afternoon, and this stillness! Where were you headed?"
"I was going to father's, but I meant to stop at Katerina Ivanovna's first."

"To her, and to father! Oh! What a coincidence! Why was I waiting for you? Hungering and thirsting for you in every corner of my soul, even in my very ribs? To send you to father and to her, to Katerina Ivanovna, so as to be done with her and with father. To send an angel. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted to send an angel. And here you are, on your way to see father and her."
"Did you really mean to send me?" cried Alyosha, his face distressed.
"Wait! You already knew it! And I can see you understand it all at once. But be quiet, quiet for now. Don't be sorry, and don't cry."
Dmitri stood up, thought a moment, and put his finger to his forehead.
"She asked you, wrote you a letter or something -- that's why you're going to her? You wouldn't be going otherwise?"
"Here's her note." Alyosha took it out of his pocket. Mitya scanned it quickly.

"And you were coming by the back way! Oh, gods, I thank you for sending him by the back way -- he's come to me like the golden fish to the poor old fisherman in the fable! Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother! Now I'm going to tell you everything, because I have to tell someone. I've already told an angel in heaven; but now I want to tell an angel on earth. You're an angel on earth. You'll hear it, and judge it, and forgive it. And that's exactly what I need -- someone above me to forgive me. Listen! If two people cut themselves loose from everything on earth and fly off into the unknown -- or at least one of them does -- and before flying off, or before going to ruin, he comes to someone else and says, 'Do this for me' -- some favor never asked before, the kind you only ask on your deathbed -- would that other person refuse, if he were a friend, or a brother?"
"I'll do it, but tell me what it is, and be quick," said Alyosha.

"Be quick! Hah!... Don't hurry, Alyosha, you're always in such a rush, fretting over things. There's no need to hurry now. The world has taken a new turn now. Ah, Alyosha, what a pity you can't understand ecstasy. But what am I saying to him? As though you didn't understand it. What a fool I am! What am I saying? 'Be noble, O man!' -- who said that?"
Alyosha decided to wait. He felt that perhaps, indeed, his purpose here lay in waiting. Mitya sank into thought for a moment, elbow on the table, head in his hand. Both were silent.

"Alyosha," said Mitya, "you're the only one who won't laugh. I'd like to begin -- my confession -- with Schiller's Hymn to Joy, An die Freude! I don't know German, I only know that's what it's called. Don't think I'm talking nonsense because I'm drunk. I'm not the least bit drunk. Brandy's fine, but it takes two bottles to get me drunk:

Silenus with his rosy phiz
Upon his stumbling ass.

But I haven't drunk a quarter of a bottle, and I'm no Silenus. I'm not Silenus, though I am strong, for I've made up my mind once and for all. Forgive me the pun; you'll have to forgive me a good deal more than puns today. Don't worry. I'm not dragging this out. I'm talking sense, and I'll get to the point in a minute. I won't keep you hanging. Wait, how does it go?"
He raised his head, thought for a minute, and began with enthusiasm:

"Wild and fearful in his cavern
Hid the naked troglodyte,
And the homeless nomad wandered
Laying waste the fertile plain.
Menacing with spear and arrow
In the woods the hunter strayed....
Woe to all poor wretches stranded
On those cruel and hostile shores!"

"From the peak of high Olympus
Came the mother Ceres down,
Seeking in those savage regions
Her lost daughter Proserpine.
But the Goddess found no refuge,
Found no kindly welcome there,
And no temple bearing witness
To the worship of the gods."

"From the fields and from the vineyards
Came no fruits to deck the feasts,
Only flesh of bloodstained victims
Smoldered on the altar-fires,
And where'er the grieving goddess
Turns her melancholy gaze,
Sunk in vilest degradation
Man his loathsomeness displays."
Mitya burst into sobs and grabbed Alyosha's hand.

"My dear, my dear, in degradation -- in degradation even now. There's a terrible amount of suffering for man on this earth, a terrible amount of trouble. Don't think I'm just some brute in an officer's uniform, wallowing in filth and drink. I hardly think of anything but that degraded man -- if I'm not lying to you. I pray to God I'm not lying, not showing off. I think about that man because I am that man myself.

Would he purge his soul from vileness
And attain to light and worth,
He must turn and cling for ever
To his ancient Mother Earth.

"But the trouble is, how am I supposed to cling forever to Mother Earth? I don't kiss her. I don't press myself to her breast. Am I supposed to become a peasant, or a shepherd? I go forward, and I don't know whether I'm heading toward shame or toward light and joy. That's the whole trouble -- everything in the world is a riddle! And whenever I've happened to sink into the vilest degradation -- and it's always been happening -- I always read that poem about Ceres and man. Has it reformed me? Never! Because I'm a Karamazov. Because when I do leap into the pit, I go headlong, heels up, and I'm pleased to be falling in that degrading position, and I take pride in it. And in the very depths of that degradation, I strike up a hymn of praise. Let me be cursed. Let me be vile and base, only let me kiss the hem of the veil in which my God is wrapped. Though I may be following the devil, I am still Your son, O Lord, and I love You, and I feel the joy without which the world could not go on standing.

Joy everlasting fostereth
The soul of all creation,
It is her secret ferment fires
The cup of life with flame.
'Tis at her beck the grass hath turned
Each blade towards the light
And solar systems have evolved
From chaos and dark night,
Filling the realms of boundless space
Beyond the sage's sight.
At bounteous Nature's kindly breast,
All things that breathe drink Joy,
And birds and beasts and creeping things
All follow where She leads.
Her gifts to man are friends in need,
The wreath, the foaming must,
To angels--vision of God's throne,
To insects--sensual lust.

"But enough poetry! I'm in tears -- let me cry. It might be foolishness, the sort of thing anyone would laugh at. But you won't laugh. Your eyes are shining too. Enough poetry. I want to tell you now about the insects to whom God gave “sensual lust.”
To insects -- sensual lust.

I am that insect, brother, and it's said of me in particular. All we Karamazovs are insects like that, and, angel that you are, that insect lives in you too, and it'll stir up a storm in your blood one day. Storms, because sensual lust is a storm -- worse than a storm! Beauty is a terrible, an awful thing! It's terrible because it can never be fathomed, and never will be, since God gives us nothing but riddles. Here the boundaries meet, and every contradiction lives side by side. I'm not an educated man, brother, but I've thought about this a great deal. There are terrifying mysteries here! Too many riddles weigh men down on this earth. We have to solve what we can, and try to come out of the water with a dry skin. Beauty! I can't stand the thought that a man of lofty mind and heart can begin with the ideal of the Madonna and end with the ideal of Sodom. What's even more terrible is that a man with the ideal of Sodom already in his soul doesn't renounce the ideal of the Madonna, and his heart can still burn for it, genuinely burn, just as it did in the days of his youth and innocence. Yes, man is broad -- too broad, really. I'd narrow him down if I could. The devil alone knows what to make of it! What's shameful to the mind is beauty, and nothing else, to the heart. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe me, for the vast mass of mankind, that's exactly where beauty is found. Did you know that secret? The terrible thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there, and the battlefield is the human heart. But a man always talks about his own particular ache. Listen, now, let's get to the facts."

title: IV. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—In Anecdote
paragraphs: "I was living a wild life back then. Father said just now that I spent several thousand roubles seducing young girls. That's a filthy invention -- there was nothing of the kind. And even if there had been, I wouldn't have needed money for that. With me, money is just an accessory, the overflow of my heart, the setting. Today she'd be my lady, tomorrow some wench off the street in her place. I entertained them both alike. I threw money away by the handful on music, carousing, gypsies. Sometimes I gave it to the ladies too, since they'll take it greedily -- no denying that -- and be pleased and grateful for it. Ladies used to be fond of me: not all of them, but it happened, it happened. But I always liked side paths, little dark back alleys off the main road -- that's where you find adventures and surprises, precious metal hidden in the dirt. I'm speaking figuratively, brother. In the town I was in, there weren't any such back alleys in the literal sense, but morally there were plenty. If you were like me, you'd know what I mean. I loved vice, I loved the disgrace of vice. I loved cruelty -- am I not a bug, am I not some noxious insect? A Karamazov, in fact! Once we all went out on a picnic, a whole crowd of us, in seven sledges. It was dark, it was winter, and I started squeezing a girl's hand, and forced her to kiss me. She was an official's daughter, a sweet, gentle, submissive creature. She let me -- let me get away with a good deal, in the dark. She thought, poor thing, that I'd come the next day to propose (I was considered a good match, too). But I didn't say a word to her for five months. I used to see her standing in a corner at dances -- we were always having dances -- her eyes fixed on me. I could see them glowing -- glowing with a kind of gentle indignation. That little game only fed the insect lust I nursed in my soul. Five months later she married an official and left town, still angry, and still, perhaps, in love with me. They live happily now, from what I hear. Notice that I told no one about it. I didn't boast of it. Even though I'm full of low desires, and love what's low, I'm not a dishonorable man. You're blushing -- your eyes just flashed. Enough of this filth for you. And really, none of that amounted to much -- roadside flowers, a la Paul de Kock -- though the cruel insect had already grown strong in my soul by then. I've got a whole album of memories like that, brother. God bless them, the darlings. I always tried to break it off without a quarrel. And I never gave any of them away. Never bragged about a single one. But that's enough of that. You can't think I brought you out here just to talk this kind of nonsense. No, I'm going to tell you something far more interesting, and don't be surprised that I'm glad to tell you, instead of being ashamed of it."
"You say that because I blushed," Alyosha said suddenly. "I wasn't blushing at what you were saying, or at what you've done. I blushed because I'm the same as you are."
"You? Come now, that's going a bit far!"

"No, it isn't too far," said Alyosha warmly (clearly this wasn't a new idea for him). "It's the same ladder. I'm on the bottom rung, and you're higher up, somewhere around the thirteenth. That's how I see it. But it's all the same thing. Exactly the same in kind. Anyone on the bottom rung is bound, sooner or later, to climb to the top one."
"Then one shouldn't step onto it at all."
"Anyone who can help it, had better not."
"But can you?"
"I don't think so."

"Hush, Alyosha, hush, my darling! I could kiss your hand, you move me so. That rogue Grushenka has an eye for men. She told me once she'd devour you one day. There, there, I won't say another word! From this field of corruption, fouled by flies, let's move on to my tragedy, also fouled by flies -- that is, by every kind of filth. Although the old man told lies about my seducing an innocent girl, there really was something of the sort in my tragedy, though it only happened once, and even then it didn't come off. The old man, who's accused me of something that never happened, doesn't even know about this actual episode; I've never told a soul about it. You're the first to hear it, except Ivan, of course -- Ivan knows everything. He's known about it for a long time, long before you did. But Ivan's a tomb."
"Ivan's a tomb?"
"Yes."
Alyosha listened with great attention.

"I was a lieutenant in a line regiment, but even so I was under supervision, more or less like a convict. And yet I was wonderfully well received in that little town. I threw money around left and right. I was thought to be rich; I thought so myself. But I must have pleased them in other ways too. Though they shook their heads over me, they liked me. My colonel, an old man, took a sudden dislike to me. He was always down on me, but I had powerful friends, and besides, the whole town was on my side, so he couldn't do me much harm. It was partly my own fault, mind you, for refusing to show him proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old fellow, who was really a very decent sort at heart, kind and hospitable, had had two wives, both dead. His first wife, who came from humble stock, had left behind a daughter as unassuming as she'd been. The daughter was a young woman of twenty-four when I was there, living with her father and an aunt, her mother's sister. The aunt was simple and uneducated; the niece was simple but full of life. I like to say nice things about people. I've never known a woman of more charming character than Agafya -- imagine, her name was Agafya Ivanovna! And she wasn't bad-looking either, in the Russian style: tall, sturdy, full-figured, with beautiful eyes, though her face was rather coarse. She'd never married, though she'd had two suitors. She turned them both down, but stayed cheerful as ever. I was close with her, but not in 'that' way -- pure friendship. I've often been friendly with women in a perfectly innocent way. I used to talk to her with shocking frankness, and she just laughed. A lot of women like that kind of freedom, and she was still a young girl too, which made it all rather amusing. Another thing -- one could never quite think of her as a 'young lady.' She and her aunt lived in her father's house with a kind of voluntary humility, never putting themselves on an equal footing with anyone else. She was a general favorite, useful to everyone, since she was a talented dressmaker. She had real talent for it. She gave her services free, without ever asking for payment, but if someone offered to pay, she didn't refuse. The colonel, of course, was another matter entirely. He was one of the leading figures in the district. He kept open house, entertained the whole town, threw suppers and dances. Right around the time I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole town was buzzing about the expected return of the colonel's second daughter, a great beauty, fresh from a fashionable boarding school in the capital. This second daughter was Katerina Ivanovna, the child of the second wife, who'd come from a distinguished general's family -- though, as I learned on good authority, she too had brought the colonel no money. She had connections, and that was all. There may have been expectations of an inheritance, but nothing had come of them.

"But when the young lady arrived home from boarding school on a visit, the whole town came alive. Our most distinguished ladies -- two 'Excellencies' and a colonel's wife -- and everyone else following their lead, immediately took her up and threw entertainments in her honor. She was the belle of every ball and picnic, and they got up tableaux vivants in aid of destitute governesses. I paid no attention, went on just as wildly as before, and one of my exploits around then set the whole town talking. I saw her taking my measure one evening at the battery commander's, but I didn't go over to her, as if I disdained making her acquaintance. I did go and speak to her later, at another evening party. She barely looked at me, and pressed her lips together scornfully. 'Wait a bit. I'll have my revenge,' I thought. I behaved like an absolute fool on a number of occasions around then, and I was well aware of it myself. What made it worse was that I could feel that 'Katenka' wasn't just some innocent little boarding-school miss, but a woman of real character, proud and genuinely high-principled; above all, she had education and intelligence, and I had neither. Do you think I meant to propose to her? No, I simply wanted revenge, because I was such a hero and she didn't seem to notice it at all.

"Meanwhile I spent my time drinking and carousing, until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Right around then father sent me six thousand roubles, in exchange for a deed in which I gave up all claims on him -- settling our accounts, so to speak, and stating that I'd expect nothing further. I didn't understand a word of it at the time. Until I came here, Alyosha, even up to these last few days, maybe even now, I've never been able to make head or tail of my money affairs with father. But never mind that, we'll get to it later.

"Just after I received the money, I got a letter from a friend telling me something that interested me enormously. The authorities, it turned out, were unhappy with our lieutenant-colonel. He was suspected of irregularities; in fact, his enemies were cooking up a surprise for him. Then the division commander arrived, and kicked up quite a storm. Shortly afterward the colonel was ordered to retire. I won't go into how it all happened. He certainly had enemies. All at once there was a noticeable coolness toward him and his whole family throughout the town. His friends all turned their backs on him. That's when I took my first step. I ran into Agafya Ivanovna, with whom I'd always been on friendly terms, and said, 'Do you know there's a shortfall of four thousand five hundred roubles of government money in your father's accounts?'
"'What do you mean? What makes you say such a thing? The general was here not long ago, and everything was fine.'
"'It was then. It isn't now.'
"She was terribly frightened.
"'Don't frighten me!' she said. 'Who told you that?'

"'Don't worry,' I said, 'I won't tell anyone. You know I'm as silent as the grave. I only wanted, in view of the "possibilities," to add that when they come to demand that four thousand five hundred roubles from your father, and he can't produce it, he'll be tried, and forced to serve as a common soldier in his old age -- unless, that is, you'd care to send me your young lady, quietly. I've just been paid. I'll give her four thousand, if you like, and keep the secret religiously.'
"'Ah, you scoundrel!' -- that's what she said. 'You wicked scoundrel! How dare you!'

"She went off in a fury, while I called after her once more that the secret would be kept sacred. Those two simple souls, Agafya and her aunt, behaved, I should say at once, like absolute angels through the whole business. They genuinely adored their 'Katya,' thought her far above them, and waited on her hand and foot. But Agafya told her about our conversation. I found that out afterward. She didn't hold it back -- and of course that was exactly what I wanted.

"Suddenly a new major arrived to take command of the battalion. The old lieutenant-colonel fell ill at once, couldn't leave his room for two days, and didn't hand over the government money. Dr. Kravchenko confirmed he really was ill. But I knew for a fact, and had known for a long time, that for the past four years the money had never actually been in his hands, except during the commander's inspection visits. He used to lend it out to a trustworthy man, a merchant in our town named Trifonov, an old widower with a big beard and gold-rimmed spectacles. Trifonov would go off to the fair, turn a tidy profit with the money, and bring back the full sum to the colonel afterward, along with a present from the fair and interest on top. But this time (I heard the whole thing quite by chance from Trifonov's son and heir, a sniveling youth, one of the most vicious in the world) -- this time, Trifonov brought nothing back from the fair at all. The lieutenant-colonel rushed to him. 'I never received any money from you, and couldn't possibly have received any,' was all the answer he got. So now our lieutenant-colonel is confined to the house, a towel round his head, with the three of them frantically applying ice to it. All of a sudden an orderly turns up with the ledger and orders him to 'hand over the battalion money immediately, within two hours.' He signed the book (I saw the signature in it afterward), stood up, said he'd go put on his uniform, ran to his bedroom, loaded his double-barreled gun with a service bullet, pulled off the boot on his right foot, pressed the gun to his chest, and started feeling for the trigger with his toe. But Agafya, remembering what I'd told her, had grown suspicious. She crept up and peeked into the room just in time. She burst in, threw herself on him from behind, wrapped her arms around him, and the gun went off, hit the ceiling, but hurt no one. The others rushed in, took the gun away, and held him by the arms. I heard all this afterward. I was at home myself, it was getting dark, and I was just about to go out. I'd dressed, brushed my hair, scented my handkerchief, and picked up my cap, when suddenly the door opened, and there in front of me stood Katerina Ivanovna.

"It's strange how these things happen sometimes. No one had seen her in the street, so no one in town knew about it. I was lodging with two decrepit old ladies who looked after me. They were the most obliging creatures, ready to do anything for me, and, at my request, afterward kept as silent as two cast-iron posts. Of course I grasped the situation at once. She walked in and looked straight at me, her dark eyes determined, even defiant, though I could see uncertainty around her lips and the corners of her mouth.
"'My sister told me,' she began, 'that you'd give me four thousand five hundred roubles if I came to you for it -- myself. I've come... give me the money!'
"She couldn't keep it up. She was out of breath, frightened, her voice failed her, and her lips and the lines around them trembled. Alyosha, are you listening, or are you asleep?"
"Mitya, I know you'll tell me the whole truth," said Alyosha, agitated.

"I'm telling it. If I tell you the whole truth, exactly as it happened, I won't spare myself. My first thought was a Karamazov one. I was bitten once by a centipede, brother, and laid up for two weeks with a fever from it. Well, I felt a centipede biting at my heart just then -- a venomous insect, you understand? I looked her up and down. You've seen her? She's a beauty. But she was beautiful in a different way back then. At that moment she was beautiful because she was noble, and I was a scoundrel; she in the full grandeur of her generosity and self-sacrifice for her father, and I -- a bug! And, scoundrel that I was, she was entirely at my mercy then, body and soul. She was trapped. I tell you honestly, that thought -- that poisonous thought -- so completely possessed my heart that it very nearly swooned under the suspense of it. It seemed as if there could be no resisting it -- as though I'd act like a bug, like a venomous spider, without a shred of pity. I could barely breathe. Understand, I ought to have gone the very next day to ask for her hand, so that it might end honorably, so to speak, so that no one could ever know, or would. Because whatever else I am, base as my desires are, I am honest. And at that very second some voice seemed to whisper in my ear: 'But when you come tomorrow to propose, that girl won't even see you; she'll have her coachman throw you out of the yard. "Tell the whole town," she'll say, "I'm not afraid of you."' I looked at the young lady, and my instinct told me it wouldn't deceive me. That's exactly how it would go, no question about it. I could see from her face already that I'd be thrown out of the house. My temper flared. I longed to play her the filthiest, most caddish trick imaginable: to look at her with a sneer, and, right there where she stood before me, crush her with the tone a shopkeeper might use.

"'Four thousand! What are you talking about? I was joking. You've been counting your chickens a little too eagerly, madam. Two hundred, if you like, gladly. But four thousand isn't a sum to be thrown away on such foolishness. You've troubled yourself for nothing.'

"I'd have lost the game, of course. She'd have fled. But it would have been an infernal revenge. It would have been worth everything. I'd have howled with regret for the rest of my life, just to have played that trick. Would you believe it, it's never happened to me with any other woman, not once, to look at her in a moment like that with such hatred. But, I swear to you, I looked at her for three seconds, maybe five, with a fearful hatred -- the kind of hatred that's only a hair's breadth from love, from the maddest love imaginable!

"I went to the window, pressed my forehead against the frozen glass, and I remember the ice burned my forehead like fire. I didn't keep her waiting long, don't worry. I turned around, went up to the table, opened the drawer, and pulled out a five-thousand-rouble banknote (it had been sitting inside a French dictionary). Then I showed it to her in silence, folded it, handed it to her, opened the door to the passage, and, stepping back, gave her a deep bow -- the most respectful, the most solemn bow, believe me! She shuddered all over, stared at me for a second, went horribly pale -- white as a sheet, in fact -- and all at once, not abruptly but softly, gently, bowed down to my feet -- not a boarding-school curtsy, but a full Russian bow, forehead to the floor. She jumped up and ran out. I was wearing my sword. I drew it and very nearly ran myself through with it right then and there -- why, I couldn't tell you. It would have been unbelievably stupid, of course. I suppose it was sheer delight. Can you understand killing yourself out of delight? But I didn't run myself through. I just kissed my sword and put it back in the scabbard -- which, by the way, there was no need for me to have mentioned. And I suspect that in telling you about my inner struggle just now I've laid it on rather thick, to glorify myself. But let it go, and to hell with anyone who pries into the human heart! Well, so much for that 'adventure' with Katerina Ivanovna. So now Ivan knows about it, and you -- no one else."

Dmitri got up, paced a step or two in his agitation, pulled out his handkerchief and mopped his forehead, then sat down again, not in his old place but on the opposite side, so that Alyosha had to turn all the way around to face him.

title: V. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—“Heels Up”
paragraphs: "Now," said Alyosha, "I understand the first half."
"You understand the first half. That half is a drama, and it played itself out back there. The second half is a tragedy, and it's being acted out right here."
"And I don't understand any of that second half yet," said Alyosha.
"And I? Do you suppose I understand it?"
"Stop, Dmitri. There's one important question. Tell me -- were you betrothed? Are you still betrothed now?"

"We weren't betrothed right away, not for three months after that whole episode. The next day I told myself the matter was closed, finished, that there'd be no sequel. It seemed caddish to me to propose to her. On her side, she gave no sign of life for the six weeks she remained in town -- except for one thing. The day after her visit, the maid slipped round with an envelope addressed to me. I tore it open: it held the change from the banknote. Only four thousand five hundred roubles had been needed, but there was a discount of about two hundred on cashing it. She sent back only about two hundred sixty. I don't remember the exact figure, but there wasn't a note, not a word of explanation. I searched the packet for a pencil mark -- n-nothing! Well, I spent the rest of the money on such a debauch that the new major felt obliged to reprimand me.

"Well, the lieutenant-colonel produced the battalion money, to everyone's astonishment, since nobody believed he still had it untouched. No sooner had he paid it than he fell ill, took to his bed, and, three weeks later, softening of the brain set in, and he died five days after that.
