He was buried with military honors, since he hadn't had time to receive his discharge. Ten days after the funeral, Katerina Ivanovna, with her aunt and sister, left for Moscow. And -- would you believe it -- on the very day they left (I hadn't seen them, didn't see them off, didn't say goodbye) I received a tiny note, a sheet of thin blue paper, with just one line on it in pencil: 'I will write to you. Wait. K.' And that was all.

"I'll explain the rest in two words now. In Moscow their fortunes changed with the speed of lightning, with all the suddenness of an Arabian fairy tale. That general's widow, their nearest relation, suddenly lost the two nieces who were her heiresses and next of kin -- both died the same week, of smallpox. The old lady, prostrate with grief, took Katya to her heart like a daughter, as her one remaining hope, clung to her, changed her will in Katya's favor. But that was all a matter for the future. In the meantime she gave her, for immediate use, eighty thousand roubles, as a marriage portion, to do with as she liked. She was a hysterical woman. I saw something of her myself in Moscow, later.

"Well, suddenly I received by post four thousand five hundred roubles. I was speechless with astonishment, as you can imagine. Three days later the promised letter arrived. I still have it with me. You must read it. She offers to be my wife, offers herself to me. 'I love you madly,' she says, 'even if you don't love me, never mind. Be my husband. Don't be afraid. I won't hold you back in any way. I'll be your chattel. I'll be the carpet under your feet. I want to love you forever. I want to save you from yourself.' Alyosha, I'm not fit to repeat those lines in my vulgar words, in my endlessly vulgar tone, that I can never cure myself of. That letter stabs me even now. Do you think I don't care -- that I don't still care? I wrote her an answer at once, since it was impossible for me to go to Moscow. I wrote to her in tears. One thing I'll be ashamed of forever. I brought up the fact that she was rich, that she had a dowry, while I was nothing but a stuck-up beggar! I mentioned money! I should have borne it in silence, but it slipped out from under my pen. Then I wrote at once to Ivan, told him everything I could in a six-page letter, and sent him to her. Why are you looking at me like that? Why are you staring? Yes, Ivan fell in love with her; he's still in love with her. I know that. I did something stupid, by the world's standards; but maybe that one stupid thing will save all of us now. Oo! Don't you see how much she thinks of Ivan, how much she respects him? When she compares the two of us, do you really think she could love a man like me?"
"But I'm convinced she loves a man like you, and not a man like him."

"She loves her own virtue, not me." The words broke from Dmitri involuntarily, almost with malice. He laughed, but a minute later his eyes flared, he flushed crimson, and struck the table violently with his fist.

"I swear, Alyosha," he cried, with real, intense anger at himself, "you may not believe me, but as God is holy, and as Christ is God, I swear that though I laughed at her lofty sentiments just now, I know that I'm a million times baser in soul than she is, and that those lofty sentiments of hers are as sincere as a heavenly angel's. That's the tragedy of it -- that I know it for certain. What if a man does show off a bit? Don't I do it myself? And yet I'm sincere -- I'm sincere. As for Ivan, I can understand how he must be cursing nature right now, with all his intellect too! To watch the preference given -- to whom, to what? To a monster, who, betrothed as he is, with everyone watching him, can't restrain his own debaucheries -- and right in front of his betrothed's own eyes! And a man like me is preferred, while he's rejected. And why? Because a girl wants to sacrifice her life and her fate out of gratitude. It's absurd! I've never said a word of this to Ivan, and of course Ivan's never dropped a hint of it to me either. But fate will run its course, and the better man will hold his ground, while the unworthy one will vanish forever into his back alley -- his filthy back alley, his beloved back alley, where he's at home, and where he'll sink into the filth and stench of his own free will, and enjoy it. I've been talking like a fool. I've got no words left. I'm using them at random, but it'll be just as I've said. I'll drown in the back alley, and she'll marry Ivan."

"Stop, Dmitri," Alyosha broke in again, deeply anxious. "There's one thing you still haven't made clear: are you still betrothed to her, after all, aren't you? How can you break off the engagement if she, your betrothed, doesn't want it broken?"

"Yes, formally and solemnly betrothed. It was all done when I first arrived in Moscow, with great ceremony, with icons, in full style. The general's widow blessed us, and -- would you believe it -- congratulated Katya. 'You've made a good choice,' she said, 'I see right through him.' And -- would you believe it -- she didn't take to Ivan at all, barely greeted him. I had a great deal of talk with Katya in Moscow. I told her about myself -- honestly, sincerely. She listened to everything.
There was sweet confusion, There were tender words.
Though there were proud words too. She wrung out of me a solemn promise to reform. I gave her my word, and here --"
"What?"
"Why, I called you out here and brought you today -- this very day, remember -- to send you -- this very day, again -- to Katerina Ivanovna, and --"
"What?"
"To tell her that I'll never come to see her again. Say, 'He sends you his compliments.'"
"But is that even possible?"
"That's exactly why I'm sending you, in my place, because it's not possible. And how could I possibly tell her myself?"
"And where are you going?"
"To the back alley."
"To Grushenka, then!" Alyosha cried mournfully, clasping his hands. "Can Rakitin really have been telling the truth? I thought you'd only just gone to visit her, and that was all."

"Can a betrothed man make visits like that? Is such a thing even possible, with a betrothed like this one, and before the eyes of the whole world? Damn it, I do have some honor! The moment I started visiting Grushenka, I stopped being betrothed, and stopped being an honest man. I understand that much. Why are you looking at me like that? You see, I went there first of all to beat her. I'd heard -- and I know it for a fact now -- that the captain, father's agent, had given Grushenka an IOU of mine, so she could sue me for payment and finish me off. They wanted to scare me. I went to beat her. I'd caught a glimpse of her before. She doesn't strike you at first sight. I knew about her old merchant, who's lying paralyzed now, but leaving her a decent little sum. I knew, too, that she was fond of money, that she hoarded it, lent it out at a wicked rate of interest, that she's a merciless cheat and swindler. I went to beat her, and I stayed. The storm broke -- it struck me down like the plague. I'm plague-stricken still, and I know that everything's over, that there'll never be anything more for me. The wheel has come full circle. That's my situation. And though I'm a beggar, as fate would have it, I had three thousand on me just then. I drove out to Mokroe with Grushenka, a place twenty-five versts from here. I got gypsies there, and champagne, and got every peasant in the place drunk on it, and all the women and girls too. I sent the thousands flying. In three days I was stripped bare, but a hero. Do you suppose the hero got what he came for? Not a sign of it from her. I tell you, that rogue Grushenka has a supple curve running through her whole body. You can see it in her little foot, even in her little toe. I saw it, and I kissed it, but that was all, I swear! 'I'll marry you if you like,' she said, 'you're a beggar, you know. Just say you won't beat me, and that you'll let me do whatever I please, and maybe I'll marry you.' She laughed, and she's laughing still!"
Dmitri leapt up in a kind of fury. He seemed all at once as though he were drunk. His eyes went suddenly bloodshot.
"And do you really mean to marry her?"

"At once, if she'll have me. And if she won't, I'll stay all the same. I'll be the porter at her gate. Alyosha!" he cried. He stopped short in front of him and, gripping him by the shoulders, began shaking him violently. "Do you understand, you innocent boy, that this is all delirium, senseless delirium, because there's a tragedy in it. Let me tell you, Alexey, that I may be a low man, with low and degraded passions, but a thief and a pickpocket Dmitri Karamazov can never be. Well, then -- let me tell you that I am a thief and a pickpocket. That very morning, just before I went to beat Grushenka, Katerina Ivanovna sent for me, and, in strict secrecy -- why, I don't know, I suppose she had her reasons -- asked me to go to the provincial capital and post three thousand roubles to Agafya Ivanovna in Moscow, so that nothing would be known of it here in town. So I had that three thousand roubles in my pocket when I went to see Grushenka, and it was that money we spent at Mokroe. Afterward I pretended I'd been to town, but I never showed her the post office receipt. I said I'd sent the money and would bring the receipt, and I still haven't brought it. I've forgotten it. Now, what do you think you're going to say to her today? 'He sends his compliments,' and she'll ask you, 'What about the money?' You might still have said to her, 'He's a degraded sensualist, a low creature, with uncontrolled passions. He didn't send your money after all, he squandered it, because, like a low brute, he couldn't control himself.' But then you could still have added, 'He isn't a thief, though. Here's your three thousand back; he's sending it back. Send it yourself to Agafya Ivanovna. But he told me to tell you, "he sends his compliments."' As it stands, though, she's going to ask, 'But where's the money?'"
"Mitya, you're unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don't worry yourself to death with despair."

"What, do you suppose I'd shoot myself just because I can't come up with three thousand to pay back? That's just it. I'm not going to shoot myself. I haven't got the strength for it now. Later, perhaps. But right now I'm going to Grushenka. I don't care what happens."
"And then what?"
"I'll be her husband, if she deigns to have me, and when her lovers come calling, I'll go into the next room. I'll clean her friends' galoshes, light their samovar, run their errands."

"Katerina Ivanovna will understand it all," Alyosha said solemnly. "She'll understand how great this trouble of yours is, and she'll forgive you. She has a noble mind, and no one could be more unhappy than you are. She'll see that for herself."
"She won't forgive everything," said Dmitri, with a grin. "There's something in it, brother, that no woman could forgive. Do you know what would be the best thing to do?"
"What?"
"Pay back the three thousand."
"Where would we even get it from? Listen, I have two thousand. Ivan will give you another thousand -- that makes three. Take it, and pay it back."

"And when would you get it -- your three thousand? You're not even of age, besides, and you must -- you absolutely must -- take my farewell to her today, with the money or without it, because I can't drag this out any longer, things have come to such a pass. Tomorrow's too late. I'm sending you to father."
"To father?"
"Yes, to father first. Ask him for three thousand."
"But, Mitya, he won't give it."
"As if he would! I know he won't. Do you know what despair means, Alexey?"
"Yes."

"Listen. Legally he owes me nothing. I've had it all from him already, I know that. But morally he owes me something, doesn't he? You know he started with twenty-eight thousand of my mother's money and turned it into a hundred thousand. Let him give me back just three of the twenty-eight thousand, and he'll pull my soul out of hell, and it'll atone for a good many of his sins. For that three thousand -- I give you my solemn word -- I'll put an end to everything, and he'll never hear from me again. This is his last chance to be a father. Tell him God himself is sending him this chance."
"Mitya, he won't give it for anything in the world."

"I know he won't. I know it perfectly well. Especially now. That's not all, either. I know something more. Just a few days ago, maybe only yesterday, he found out for the first time -- in earnest (underline in earnest) -- that Grushenka really isn't joking, and really does mean to marry me. He knows her nature; he knows the cat he's dealing with. And do you suppose he's going to hand me money to help bring that about, when he's crazy about her himself? And that's still not all. I can tell you more. I know that for the past five days he's had three thousand drawn out of the bank, changed into hundred-rouble notes, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals, and tied across with red tape. You see how well I know all about it! On the envelope it says: 'To my angel, Grushenka, whenever she comes to me.' He scrawled that himself, in silence, in secret, and no one knows the money's there except the valet, Smerdyakov, whom he trusts like himself. So now he's been waiting for Grushenka for the last three or four days; he's hoping she'll come for the money. He's sent word to her about it, and she's sent word back that maybe she'll come. And if she does go to the old man, how can I possibly marry her after that? Now you understand why I'm here in secret, and what I'm keeping watch for."
"For her?"

"Yes, for her. Foma has a room in the house where these women live. Foma's from our parts; he served in our regiment. He does odd jobs for them. He's the night watchman, and goes grouse-shooting during the day; that's how he lives. I've set myself up in his room. Neither he nor the women of the house know the secret -- that I'm keeping watch here."
"No one but Smerdyakov knows, then?"
"No one else. He'll let me know if she goes to the old man."
"It was he who told you about the money, then?"

"Yes. It's a dead secret. Even Ivan doesn't know about the money, or anything else. The old man's sending Ivan off to Tchermashnya for two or three days. A buyer's turned up for the copse -- he'll give eight thousand for the timber. So the old man keeps begging Ivan to help him by going to settle it. It'll take him two or three days. That's exactly what the old man wants, so Grushenka can come while he's away."
"Then he's expecting Grushenka today?"

"No, she won't come today; there are signs. She's certainly not coming," Mitya cried suddenly. "Smerdyakov thinks so too. Father's drinking right now. He's sitting at the table with Ivan. Go to him, Alyosha, and ask him for the three thousand."
"Mitya, dear, what's the matter with you?" cried Alyosha, jumping up from his seat, looking sharply at his brother's frenzied face. For a moment it struck him that Dmitri had gone mad.
"What is it? I'm not insane," said Dmitri, looking at him intently and earnestly. "No fear of that. I'm sending you to father, and I know exactly what I'm saying. I believe in miracles."
"In miracles?"
"In a miracle of Divine Providence. God knows my heart. He sees my despair. He sees the whole picture. Surely he won't let something terrible happen. Alyosha, I believe in miracles. Go!"
"I'm going. Tell me, will you wait for me here?"

"Yes. I know it'll take some time. You can't just walk up and ask him outright. He's drunk now. I'll wait three hours -- four, five, six, seven. Only remember, you have to go to Katerina Ivanovna today, even if it's midnight, with the money or without it, and say, 'He sends his compliments to you.' I want you to say that exact phrase to her: 'He sends his compliments to you.'"
"Mitya! And what if Grushenka comes today -- or if not today, tomorrow, or the day after?"
"Grushenka? I'll see her. I'll rush out and stop it."
"And if --"
"If there's an if, it'll be murder. I couldn't bear it."
"Who'll be murdered?"
"The old man. I won't kill her."
"Brother, what are you saying?"

"Oh, I don't know.... I don't know. Maybe I won't kill him, and maybe I will. I'm afraid he'll suddenly become so loathsome to me, with that face of his at that moment. I hate his ugly throat, his nose, his eyes, his shameless smirk. I feel a physical revulsion. That's what I'm afraid of. That's what might be too much for me."
"I'll go, Mitya. I believe God will make things turn out for the best, that nothing terrible will happen."
"And I'll sit and wait for the miracle. And if it doesn't happen --"
Alyosha walked toward his father's house, deep in thought.

title: VI. Smerdyakov
paragraphs: He did in fact find his father still at the table. Though there was a dining room in the house, the table was laid, as usual, in the drawing room, which was the largest room, furnished with old-fashioned ostentation. The furniture was white, very old, upholstered in old red silk. Between the windows stood mirrors in elaborate white-and-gilt frames, carved in the old style. The walls, covered in white paper torn in many places, held two large portraits -- one of some prince who'd been governor of the district thirty years before, the other of some bishop, also long dead. In the corner opposite the door stood several icons, before which a lamp was lit at nightfall -- not so much for devotional purposes as to light the room. Fyodor Pavlovitch used to go to bed very late, at three or four in the morning, and would wander about the room at night, or sit in an armchair, thinking. This had become a habit of his. He often slept entirely alone in the house, sending the servants off to the lodge; but usually Smerdyakov stayed behind, sleeping on a bench in the hall.

When Alyosha came in, dinner was over, but coffee and preserves had been brought out. Fyodor Pavlovitch liked sweet things with brandy after dinner. Ivan was at the table too, sipping coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood nearby. Both the gentlemen and the servants seemed in unusually good spirits. Fyodor Pavlovitch was roaring with laughter. Before Alyosha even entered the room, he heard that shrill laugh he knew so well, and could tell from the sound of it that his father had only reached the good-humored stage, and was still far from fully drunk.

"Here he is! Here he is!" Fyodor Pavlovitch yelled, thrilled at the sight of Alyosha. "Join us. Sit down. Coffee's a lenten dish, but it's hot and good. I won't offer you brandy, you're keeping the fast. But would you like some anyway? No -- better yet, I'll give you some of our famous liqueur. Smerdyakov, go to the cupboard, second shelf on the right. Here are the keys. Look sharp!"
Alyosha began refusing the liqueur.
"Never mind. If you won't have it, we will," said Fyodor Pavlovitch, beaming. "But wait -- have you had dinner?"
"Yes," Alyosha answered, though in truth he'd only eaten a piece of bread and drunk a glass of kvas in the Father Superior's kitchen. "Though I'd be glad of some hot coffee."

"Bravo, my darling! He'll have some coffee. Does it need warming up? No, it's boiling. It's capital coffee -- Smerdyakov's making. My Smerdyakov's an artist with coffee, and with fish pies too, and fish soup. You must come one day and have some fish soup. Just let me know beforehand.... But wait -- didn't I tell you this morning to come home with your mattress and pillow and all? Have you brought your mattress? He he he!"
"No, I haven't," said Alyosha, smiling too.

"Ah, but you were scared, weren't you, this morning? There, my darling, I couldn't do anything to upset you. Do you know, Ivan, I can't resist the way he looks a man straight in the face and laughs? It makes me laugh all over. I'm so fond of him. Alyosha, let me give you my blessing -- a father's blessing."
Alyosha rose, but Fyodor Pavlovitch had already changed his mind.

"No, no," he said. "I'll just make the sign of the cross over you, for now. Sit still. Now we've got a treat for you -- right up your alley, too. It'll make you laugh. Balaam's ass has started talking to us here -- and how he talks! How he talks!"

Balaam's ass, it turned out, was the valet, Smerdyakov. He was a young man of about twenty-four, remarkably unsociable and taciturn. Not that he was shy or bashful. Quite the opposite -- he was conceited, and seemed to despise everybody.

But we should pause here and say a few words about him. He'd been raised by Grigory and Marfa, but the boy had grown up "with no sense of gratitude," as Grigory put it; he was an unfriendly boy, and seemed to look at the world with mistrust. As a child he'd loved hanging cats and burying them with great ceremony. He'd dress himself in a sheet, as though it were a surplice, and sing, waving some object over the dead cat as though it were a censer. He did all this secretly, on the sly, with the greatest care. Grigory once caught him at this game and gave him a sound beating. He shrank into a corner and sulked there for a week. "He doesn't care for you or me, the little monster," Grigory used to say to Marfa, "and he doesn't care for anyone." "Are you even a human being?" he'd say, addressing the boy directly. "You're not a human being. You grew out of the mildew in the bathhouse. That's what you are." Smerdyakov, it turned out later, never forgave him those words. Grigory taught him to read and write, and when he was twelve began teaching him Scripture. But this instruction went nowhere. At the second or third lesson the boy suddenly grinned.
"What's that for?" asked Grigory, glaring at him threateningly from under his spectacles.
"Oh, nothing. God created light on the first day, and the sun, moon, and stars on the fourth day. Where did the light come from on the first day?"

Grigory was thunderstruck. The boy looked at his teacher with something close to mockery. There was something downright condescending in his expression. Grigory couldn't restrain himself. "I'll show you where!" he shouted, and gave the boy a violent slap across the cheek. The boy took the slap without a word, but withdrew into his corner again for several days. A week later he had his first attack of the illness that would afflict him for the rest of his life -- epilepsy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard of it, his attitude toward the boy seemed to change at once. Until then he'd taken no notice of him, though he never scolded him either, and always gave him a copeck whenever he passed him. Sometimes, when he was in a good mood, he'd send the boy something sweet from his own table. But the moment he heard about the illness, he took an active interest in him, sent for a doctor, tried remedies -- but the disease proved incurable. The fits came, on average, once a month, though at varying intervals, and varied in severity too -- some light, some very severe. Fyodor Pavlovitch strictly forbade Grigory to lay a hand on the boy again, and began letting him come upstairs. For a time he also forbade anyone to teach him anything at all. One day, when the boy was about fifteen, Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed him lingering by the bookcase, reading the titles through the glass. Fyodor Pavlovitch owned a fair number of books -- over a hundred -- though no one had ever seen him actually read one. He handed Smerdyakov the key to the bookcase at once. "Here, read. You'll be my librarian. Better sitting and reading than hanging around the yard. Here, read this," and Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka.
He read a little of it but didn't like it. He never once smiled, and ended up frowning.
"Why? Isn't it funny?" asked Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Smerdyakov said nothing.
"Answer me, stupid!"
"It's all made up," the boy mumbled, with a grin.
"Then go to the devil! You've got the soul of a lackey. Wait, here's Smaragdov's Universal History. That one's all true. Read that."
But Smerdyakov didn't get through ten pages of Smaragdov. He found it dull. So the bookcase was shut again.

Shortly afterward, Marfa and Grigory reported to Fyodor Pavlovitch that Smerdyakov was developing an unusual fussiness about his food. He'd sit before his soup, pick up his spoon, and peer down into the bowl, bending over it, examining it, taking a spoonful and holding it up to the light.
"What is it? A beetle?" Grigory would ask.
"A fly, perhaps," Marfa would observe.

The squeamish young man never answered, but he did the same thing with his bread, his meat, everything he ate. He'd hold a piece up to the light on his fork, scrutinize it under close inspection, and only after long deliberation decide whether to put it in his mouth.
"Ach! Fine gentleman's airs!" Grigory muttered, watching him.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about this new development in Smerdyakov, he decided to make him his cook, and sent him off to Moscow to train. He spent several years there and came back remarkably changed in appearance. He looked strangely old for his age. His face had grown wrinkled, sallow, and oddly sexless. In character, he seemed almost exactly as he'd been before he left. Just as unsociable, showing not the slightest inclination toward company of any kind. In Moscow too, as we heard afterward, he'd stayed silent the whole time. Moscow itself hadn't interested him much; he'd seen very little of it, and paid scarcely any attention to anything. He went to the theater once, but came back silent and displeased with it. On the other hand, he returned from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. He brushed his clothes meticulously, twice a day without fail, and loved polishing his smart calfskin boots with a special English polish, until they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, nearly all of which Smerdyakov spent on clothes, pomade, perfume, and things of that sort. But he seemed to have as much contempt for women as for men; he was reserved, almost unapproachable, around them. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to see him differently after that. His fits were growing more frequent, and on the days he was ill, Marfa did the cooking, which didn't suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.
"Why are your fits getting worse?" Fyodor Pavlovitch asked, eyeing his new cook sideways. "Want to get married? Should I find you a wife?"

But Smerdyakov turned pale with anger and made no reply. Fyodor Pavlovitch left him alone with an impatient wave. The important thing was that he had complete confidence in his honesty. It happened once, when Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk, that he dropped three hundred-rouble notes -- just received -- in the muddy courtyard. He didn't notice until the next day, and was just about to search his pockets when he saw the notes lying on the table. Where had they come from? Smerdyakov had picked them up and brought them in the day before.

"Well, my lad, I've never met anyone like you," Fyodor Pavlovitch said curtly, and gave him ten roubles. We might add that he not only believed in his honesty, but had, for some reason, taken a liking to him, though the young man looked at him just as sullenly as he looked at everyone else, and was always silent. He rarely spoke. If anyone had wondered, back then, what the young man was interested in, what was going on in his mind, it would have been impossible to tell just by looking at him. And yet he'd sometimes stop suddenly, in the house, or even in the yard or the street, and stand still for ten minutes, lost in thought. A physiognomist studying his face would have said there was no thought in it, no reflection at all, just a kind of contemplation. There's a remarkable painting by the painter Kramskoy called Contemplation. There's a forest in winter, and on a road through the forest, in absolute solitude, stands a peasant in a torn kaftan and bark shoes. He stands as though lost in thought. But he isn't thinking; he's "contemplating." If someone touched him, he'd start and look up as though waking, bewildered. True, he'd come to himself again immediately; but if you asked him what he'd been thinking about, he'd remember nothing. And yet, probably, hidden away inside him, is the impression that dominated him during that period of contemplation. Those impressions are dear to him, and no doubt he hoards them, imperceptibly, even unconsciously. How, and why, he couldn't say himself. He might, after hoarding impressions for years on end, suddenly abandon everything and set off on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, for the salvation of his soul, or perhaps he'll suddenly set fire to his native village, or perhaps do both. There are plenty of these "contemplatives" among the peasantry. Well, Smerdyakov was probably one of them, and was probably greedily hoarding up his own impressions, hardly knowing why.

title: VII. The Controversy
paragraphs: But Balaam's ass had suddenly spoken. The subject was a strange one. Grigory had gone out that morning to buy provisions, and had heard from the shopkeeper Lukyanov the story of a Russian soldier that had appeared in that day's newspaper. This soldier had been taken prisoner somewhere in a remote part of Asia, and was threatened with immediate, agonizing death if he didn't renounce Christianity and convert to Islam. He refused to deny his faith, and was tortured, flayed alive, and died praising and glorifying Christ. Grigory had told the story at the table. Fyodor Pavlovitch always liked, over dessert after dinner, to laugh and talk, even if only with Grigory. That afternoon he was in a particularly good-humored, expansive mood. Sipping his brandy and listening to the story, he remarked that they ought to make a saint out of a soldier like that, and send his skin off to some monastery. "That would draw the crowds, and bring in the money."

Grigory frowned, seeing that Fyodor Pavlovitch was nowhere near touched, but, as usual, was starting up his mockery. At that moment Smerdyakov, who was standing by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often waited at table toward the end of dinner, and had done so every day since Ivan's arrival in town.
"What are you grinning at?" asked Fyodor Pavlovitch, catching the smile at once, and knowing it was aimed at Grigory.

"Well, in my opinion," Smerdyakov began, suddenly and unexpectedly, in a loud voice, "if that praiseworthy soldier's feat was really so great, there'd have been, to my mind, no sin in it if, faced with such an emergency, he'd renounced, so to speak, the name of Christ and his own christening, in order to save his life by that same means -- so as to make up for his cowardice, over the years, through good deeds."
"How could it not be a sin? You're talking nonsense. For that you'll go straight to hell and be roasted there like mutton," Fyodor Pavlovitch put in.
It was at this point that Alyosha came in, and Fyodor Pavlovitch, as we've seen, was delighted at his arrival.
"We're on your subject, your very subject," he chuckled gleefully, making Alyosha sit down to listen.
"As for the mutton, that's not so, and there'll be nothing of the sort waiting there for it, and there shouldn't be either, if it's according to justice," Smerdyakov maintained stoutly.
"How do you mean, 'according to justice'?" cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, even more gleeful now, nudging Alyosha with his knee.
"He's a rascal, that's what he is!" burst from Grigory. He glared at Smerdyakov furiously.

"As for being a rascal, just wait a little, Grigory Vassilyevitch," Smerdyakov answered with perfect composure. "You'd better consider it for yourself -- once I'm taken prisoner by the enemies of the Christian race, and they demand that I curse the name of God and renounce my holy christening, I'm fully entitled to act on my own judgment, since there'd be no sin in it at all."
"But you've said that already. Don't waste words. Prove it," cried Fyodor Pavlovitch.
"Soup-maker!" Grigory muttered contemptuously.

"As for being a soup-maker, wait a bit too, and consider it for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch, without abusing me. Because the moment I say to those enemies, 'No, I'm not a Christian, and I curse my true God,' then at once, by God's own high judgment, I become immediately and specifically anathema accursed, and I'm cut off from the Holy Church, exactly as though I were a heathen -- so that at that very instant, not only the moment I say it aloud, but the moment I think of saying it, before even a quarter of a second has passed, I'm already cut off. Is that so, or not, Grigory Vassilyevitch?"
He addressed Grigory with obvious satisfaction, though he was really answering Fyodor Pavlovitch's questions, and was well aware of it, deliberately pretending it was Grigory who'd asked them.
"Ivan," Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly cried, "lean down, let me whisper to you. He's put on this whole performance for your benefit. He wants you to praise him. Praise him."
Ivan listened with perfect seriousness to his father's excited whisper.
"Wait, Smerdyakov, be quiet a moment," Fyodor Pavlovitch cried again. "Ivan, your ear again."
Ivan bent down once more, his face perfectly grave.
"I love you just as much as Alyosha. Don't think I don't love you. Some brandy?"
"Yes -- but you're rather drunk yourself," thought Ivan, looking steadily at his father.
He was watching Smerdyakov with great curiosity.
"You're already anathema accursed," Grigory suddenly burst out, "and how dare you argue, you rascal, after that, if --"
"Don't scold him, Grigory, don't scold him," Fyodor Pavlovitch cut him off.

"You should wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch, just a little while, and listen, because I haven't finished all I had to say. Because at the very moment I become accursed, that same highest moment, I become exactly like a heathen, and my christening is lifted off me and becomes worthless. Isn't that so?"
"Get on with it, finish it, my boy," Fyodor Pavlovitch urged him, sipping from his wineglass with relish.

"And if I've stopped being a Christian, then I told no lie to the enemy when they asked whether I was a Christian or not, since I'd already been relieved by God himself of my Christianity, by the thought alone, before I'd even had time to say a word to the enemy. And if I've already been discharged, in what manner, and with what kind of justice, could I be held responsible as a Christian in the other world, for having denied Christ, when, through the very thought alone, before denying him, I'd already been relieved of my christening? If I'm no longer a Christian, then I can't renounce Christ, since I've got nothing left to renounce. Who's going to hold an unclean Tatar responsible, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even in heaven, for not having been born a Christian? And who would punish him for that, seeing as you can't skin the same ox twice? Because God Almighty himself, even if he did hold the Tatar responsible, would, I imagine, give him the smallest possible punishment when he dies (since he has to be punished somehow), judging that he isn't to blame for having come into the world an unclean heathen, born of heathen parents. Surely the Lord God can't just take a Tatar and declare he was a Christian? That would mean the Almighty was telling an outright lie. And can the Lord of heaven and earth tell a lie, even in a single word?"

Grigory was thunderstruck, and stared at the speaker, his eyes nearly starting out of his head. Though he didn't clearly understand what had been said, he'd caught something in this whole rigmarole, and stood there looking like a man who's just knocked his head against a wall. Fyodor Pavlovitch emptied his glass and burst into his shrill laugh.

"Alyosha! Alyosha! What do you say to that! Ah, you casuist! He must have picked that up from the Jesuits somewhere, Ivan. Oh, you stinking Jesuit, who taught you that? But you're talking nonsense, you casuist, nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Don't cry, Grigory, we'll reduce him to smoke and ashes in a moment. Tell me this, O ass -- you may be right in front of your enemies, but you've renounced your faith all the same in your own heart, and by your own account, in that very hour you became anathema accursed. And once you're anathema, they won't be patting you on the head for it down in hell. What do you say to that, my fine Jesuit?"
"There's no doubt I renounced it in my own heart, but there was no particular sin in that. Or if there was sin, it was only the most ordinary kind."
"How's that the most ordinary?"
"You lie, accursed one!" hissed Grigory.

"Consider it yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch," Smerdyakov went on, calm and unruffled, well aware of his triumph, but generous toward his defeated opponent, as it were. "Consider it yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch: it's written in Scripture that if you have faith, even as small as a mustard seed, and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move, without the slightest delay, at your command. Well then, Grigory Vassilyevitch, if I'm without faith, and you have faith so great that you're forever cursing at me over it, then you go ahead and try telling this mountain -- not to move into the sea, that's a long way off -- but even into our own stinking little river running at the bottom of the garden. You'll see for yourself it won't budge, but will stay exactly where it is, no matter how much you shout at it, and that proves, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you don't have faith in the proper manner, and just go around abusing other people about it. And another thing -- taking into account that nowadays no one, not only you, but truly no one, from the highest person down to the lowest peasant, is able to shove mountains into the sea -- except maybe one man in the whole world, or two at most, and they're most likely off saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you'd never even find them -- if that's how it is, if everyone else lacks faith, will God curse the whole rest of them? That is, the entire population of the earth, except for those two hermits in the desert -- and in his well-known mercy, will he not forgive a single one of them? And so I'm convinced that even though I may have doubted once, I'll be forgiven, if I shed tears of repentance."
"Stay!" cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, in a transport of delight. "So you're saying there are two who can move mountains? Ivan, make a note of that, write it down. There you have the Russian all over!"
"You're quite right, it's characteristic of the people's faith," Ivan agreed, with an approving smile.
"You agree. Then it must be true, if you agree. It's true, isn't it, Alyosha? That's the Russian faith all over, isn't it?"
"No, Smerdyakov doesn't have the Russian faith at all," said Alyosha, firmly and gravely.
"I'm not talking about his faith. I mean the idea of those two in the desert, just the idea itself. Surely that's Russian, isn't it?"
"Yes, that's purely Russian," said Alyosha, smiling.

"Your words are worth a gold piece, O ass, and I'll give it to you today. But as for the rest, it's nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Let me tell you, stupid, that all of us here have little faith, only out of carelessness, because we haven't the time; things press on us too much, and, in the second place, the Lord God has only given us twenty-four hours in the day, so that a man barely has time to get enough sleep, let alone repent of his sins. While you went and denied your faith to your enemies, when you'd nothing else in the world to think about except showing that faith! So I reckon, brother, that it does constitute a sin."

"Constitute a sin it may, but consider it for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that it only lessens the sin, if it constitutes one at all. If I'd truly believed then, as I ought to have believed, it really would have been sinful of me not to face torture for my faith, and to go over instead to the pagan Mohammedan faith. But then, of course, it would never have come to torture at all, because at that very instant I'd only have had to say to the mountain, 'Move, and crush the tormentor,' and it would have moved, and at that very instant crushed him like a black beetle, and I'd have walked away as though nothing had happened, praising and glorifying God. But suppose, at that very moment, I'd tried all that, and cried out to the mountain, 'Crush these tormentors,' and it hadn't crushed them -- how could I help doubting, pray, at a moment like that, at such a dreadful hour of mortal terror? And apart from that, I'd already know that I couldn't attain the fullness of the Kingdom of Heaven anyway (since, if the mountain hadn't moved at my word, they couldn't have thought too highly of my faith up above, and there could be no very great reward waiting for me in the world to come). So why should I let them flay the skin off my back too, to no purpose at all? Because even if they'd flayed half the skin off my back, the mountain still wouldn't have moved at my word or at my cry. And at such a moment, not only might doubt come over a man, he might lose his reason entirely from fear, so that he couldn't think at all. And so how could I be especially to blame, if, seeing no advantage or reward for myself either here or there, I chose, at the very least, to save my own skin? And so, trusting fully in the grace of the Lord, I'd cherish the hope that I might be forgiven altogether."

title: VIII. Over The Brandy
paragraphs: The argument was over. But, strangely enough, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who'd been in such high spirits, suddenly began to frown. He frowned and gulped down brandy -- and it was already one glass too many.

"Get out of here, you Jesuits!" he shouted at the servants. "Go away, Smerdyakov. I'll send you the gold piece I promised you today, but be off! Don't cry, Grigory. Go to Marfa, she'll comfort you and put you to bed. The rascals won't even let us sit in peace after dinner," he snapped irritably, as the servants promptly withdrew at his word.
"Smerdyakov always pokes his way in now, after dinner. You're the one he's so interested in. What have you done to fascinate him?" he added, turning to Ivan.
"Nothing whatever," Ivan answered. "He's pleased to think highly of me; he's a lackey, and a shabby soul. Raw material for revolution, though, when the time comes."
"For revolution?"
"There'll be others, better ones. But there'll be some like him too. His kind will come first, and better ones after."
"And when will that time come?"
"The rocket will go up and fizzle out, most likely. The peasants aren't too fond of listening to these soup-makers yet, at least not so far."
"Ah, brother, but a Balaam's ass like that thinks and thinks, and God only knows where he'll end up."
"He's storing up ideas," said Ivan, smiling.

"You see, I know he can't stand me, or anyone else, even you, though you imagine he thinks highly of you. Worse still with Alyosha -- he despises Alyosha. But he doesn't steal, that's one thing in his favor, and he's no gossip, he holds his tongue, doesn't air our dirty linen in public. He makes a capital fish pie, too. But damn him, is he really worth all this talk?"
"Of course he isn't."

"And as for whatever ideas he might be hatching -- the Russian peasant, generally speaking, needs a good thrashing. That's what I've always maintained. Our peasants are swindlers, and don't deserve any pity, and it's a good thing they're still flogged sometimes. Russia's rich in birch trees. If we ever cut down the forests, it'd be the ruin of Russia. I stand up for clever people. We've stopped thrashing the peasants -- we've grown too refined for that -- but they go right on thrashing each other. And a good thing too. 'For with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again,' or however it goes. Anyway, it'll be measured out to them. But Russia's all swinishness, through and through. My dear boy, if you only knew how much I hate Russia.... That is, not Russia itself, but all this vice! But maybe I do mean Russia. Tout cela c'est de la cochonnerie.... Do you know what I like? I like wit."
"You've had another glass. That's enough."

"Wait a bit. I'll have one more, then another, and then I'll stop. No, wait, you interrupted me. Back at Mokroe I was talking to an old man, and he told me: 'There's nothing we like so much as sentencing girls to a thrashing, and we always give the lads the job of doing it. And the girl he's thrashed today, the young man will propose to tomorrow. So it suits the girls just fine, too,' he said. There's a set of de Sades for you! But it's clever all the same. Shall we go over and have a look at that sort of thing sometime, eh? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don't be bashful, child. I'm sorry I didn't stay to dinner at the Superior's and tell the monks all about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don't be angry that I offended your Superior this morning. I lost my temper. If there is a God, if he exists, then of course I'm to blame, and I'll have to answer for it. But if there's no God at all, then what do your fathers deserve? It's not enough to cut their heads off, since they hold back progress. Would you believe it, Ivan, that all this really tears at my feelings? No, I can see you don't believe it, from your eyes. You believe what people say -- that I'm nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I'm nothing but a buffoon?"
"No, I don't believe it."

"And I believe that you don't, and that you're speaking the truth. You look sincere, and you speak sincerely. But not Ivan. Ivan's supercilious.... I'd still put an end to your monks, all the same. I'd take that whole mystical business and stamp it out, once and for all, everywhere in Russia, to bring all the fools to their senses. And think of the gold and silver that would come pouring into the mint!"
"But why suppress it?" asked Ivan.
"So that Truth may prevail. That's why."
"Well, if Truth were to prevail, you know, you'd be the very first one robbed and suppressed."

"Ah! I daresay you're right. Ah, what an ass I am!" Fyodor Pavlovitch burst out, striking himself lightly on the forehead. "Well, your monastery can stand then, Alyosha, if that's how it is. And we clever people will sit snug and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, it must have been ordained that way by the Almighty himself. Ivan, tell me -- is there a God, or isn't there? Wait, tell me the truth, tell me seriously. Why are you laughing again?"
"I'm laughing because you made such a clever remark just now, about Smerdyakov's belief in the existence of two saints who could move mountains."
"Why, am I like him now, then?"
"Very much so."

"Well, that just shows I'm a Russian too, and I've got a Russian characteristic in me. And you might get caught the same way, philosopher though you are. Want to bet I'll catch you at it tomorrow? Tell me anyway -- is there a God, or isn't there? Only be serious. I want you to be serious now."
"No, there is no God."
"Alyosha, is there a God?"
"There is."
"Ivan, and is there any kind of immortality -- just a little, just a tiny bit?"
"There's no immortality either."
"None at all?"
"None at all."
"So it's absolute nothingness, then. Or maybe there's just something? Anything's better than nothing!"
"Absolute nothingness."
"Alyosha, is there immortality?"
"There is."
"God and immortality?"
"God and immortality. Immortality is in God."

"Hm! It's more likely Ivan's right. Good Lord, to think how much faith, how much strength of every kind, mankind has poured out for nothing, on that dream, and for how many thousand years. Who's it who's laughing at man? Ivan! For the last time, once and for all -- is there a God, or isn't there? I'm asking you for the last time!"
"And for the last time -- there isn't."
"Who's laughing at mankind, Ivan?"
"It must be the devil," said Ivan, smiling.
"And the devil? Does he exist?"
"No, there's no devil either."
"That's a pity. Damn it all, what wouldn't I do to the man who first invented God! Hanging on a bitter aspen tree would be too good for him."
"There'd have been no civilization at all if they hadn't invented God."
"Wouldn't there have been? Without God?"
"No. And there'd have been no brandy either. But I really must take your brandy away from you now."
"Stop, stop, stop, dear boy, just one more little glass. I've hurt Alyosha's feelings. You're not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!"
"No, I'm not angry. I know your thoughts. Your heart is better than your head."
"My heart better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And that, from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?"
"Yes."

"You must love him" (Fyodor Pavlovitch was very drunk by this point). "Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was worked up. Still, there's something witty about that elder, don't you think, Ivan?"
"Very likely."

"There is, there is. Il y a du Piron là-dedans. He's a Jesuit, a Russian one, mind you. Being an honorable man, he's got some hidden indignation boiling inside him at having to keep up the pretense of holiness."
"But he believes in God, of course."

"Not a bit of it. Didn't you know? Why, he tells everyone so himself. That is, not everyone -- just the clever people who come to see him. He said straight out to Governor Schultz not long ago: 'Credo, but I don't know in what.'"
"Really?"

"He really did say that. But I respect him. There's something of Mephistopheles about him, or rather of 'The Hero of Our Time' -- Arbenin, or whatever his name is.... You see, he's a sensualist. Such a sensualist, in fact, that I'd be afraid for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he invited us to tea, tea with liqueur -- the ladies send him liqueur -- and started telling us about the old days until we nearly split our sides laughing.... Especially about the time he cured a paralyzed woman. 'If my legs weren't so bad, I know a dance I could show you,' he said. What do you make of that? 'I've had plenty of tricks up my sleeve in my time,' he said. He swindled Demidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand."
"What, he stole it?"

"He brought him the money like a man he trusted, saying, 'Take care of this for me, friend, there'll be a police search at my place tomorrow.' And he kept it. 'You gave it to the Church,' he told him. I said to him: 'You're a scoundrel,' I said. 'No,' he said, 'I'm not a scoundrel, I'm just broad-minded.' But that wasn't him -- that was someone else. I've mixed him up with someone else... without even noticing. Come, one more glass and that's enough. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I've been telling lies. Why didn't you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?"
"I knew you'd stop on your own."
"That's a lie. You did it out of spite, out of plain spite against me. You despise me. You've come here and despised me in my own house."
"Well, I'm leaving. You've had too much brandy."
"I've begged you, for Christ's sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won't go."
"I'll go tomorrow if you're so set on it."
"You won't go. You want to keep an eye on me. That's what you want, spiteful fellow. That's exactly why you won't go."
The old man kept at it. He'd reached that stage of drunkenness where a normally inoffensive drunk starts trying to pick a quarrel and assert himself.

"Why are you looking at me like that? Why do you look at me that way? Your eyes say, 'You ugly drunkard!' Your eyes are full of mistrust. They're contemptuous.... You've come here with some scheme in mind. Alyosha, here, looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn't despise me. Alexey, you mustn't love Ivan."
"Don't be so hard on my brother. Leave off attacking him," Alyosha said firmly.
"Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take the brandy away, Ivan. That's the third time I've told you."
He fell into thought, and suddenly a slow, cunning grin spread across his face.

"Don't be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don't love me, but don't be angry all the same. You've got nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I'll come and visit you myself and bring you a present. I'll show you a little wench there. I've had my eye on her a long while. She still runs around barefoot. Don't be put off by barefoot wenches -- don't despise them -- they're pearls!"
And he kissed his own hand with a smack.

"To my mind," he revived at once, seeming to grow sober the instant he touched on his favorite topic, "to my mind... Ah, you boys! You children, little sucking pigs, to my mind... I've never thought a woman ugly in my whole life -- that's been my rule! Can you understand that? How could you possibly understand it? You've got milk in your veins, not blood. You haven't even hatched yet. My rule has always been that you can find something devilishly interesting in every single woman, something you won't find in any other. Only you have to know how to find it -- that's the whole trick! That's a real talent! To my mind there's no such thing as an ugly woman. The simple fact that she's a woman is half the battle right there... but how could you understand that? Even in old maids, even in them you can discover something that makes you wonder how men could have been such fools as to let them grow old without ever noticing them. Barefoot girls, or plain ones -- you have to catch them off guard. Didn't you know that? You have to astonish them until they're dazzled, thrown off balance, ashamed that a gentleman like you could possibly fall for a little nobody like her. It's a fine thing that there always have been, and always will be, masters and servants in this world, so there'll always be some little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that's really all a man needs for happiness. Wait... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother, but in a different way. I'd pay her no attention at all, and then, all at once, when the moment came, I'd turn into pure devotion, crawl on my knees, kiss her feet, and I always, always -- I remember it like it was yesterday -- reduced her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, odd little laugh of hers. It was peculiar to her. I knew her attacks always started that way. The next day she'd start shrieking hysterically, and that little laugh wasn't a sign of pleasure at all, though it made a very convincing imitation of one. That's the great trick -- knowing how to handle every single person. Once a man named Belyavsky -- handsome fellow, and rich -- used to like coming round here and hanging about her -- suddenly gave me a slap across the face, right in front of her. And she -- meek as a lamb -- why, I thought she'd have knocked me flat for that blow. How she went at me! 'You've been struck, struck!' she said. 'You've taken a blow from him. You were trying to sell me to him,' she said.... 'And how dare he strike you in front of me! Never come near me again, never, never! Go at once, challenge him to a duel!' I took her to the monastery after that, to bring her back to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear to God, Alyosha, I never once insulted the poor crazy girl! Except once, maybe, that first year. She was very fond of praying back then. She used to observe the feasts of Our Lady especially, and would turn me out of her room on those days. I'll knock that mysticism right out of her, I thought! 'Here,' I said, 'you see this holy image of yours. Here it is. I'm taking it down. You believe it's miraculous, but here, I'll spit on it right now and nothing will happen to me for it!'... When she saw that, good Lord! I thought she'd kill me. But she just jumped up, wrung her hands, then suddenly buried her face in them, started shaking all over, and collapsed to the floor... fell in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what's the matter?"

The old man jumped up in alarm. From the moment he'd started speaking about his mother, Alyosha's face had gradually changed. He'd flushed crimson, his eyes were glowing, his lips trembling. The old sot had gone rambling on, oblivious to all of it, until the moment when something very strange happened to Alyosha. What he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly repeated in Alyosha, exactly. He jumped up from his seat exactly as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, buried his face in them, and fell back into his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, silent, violent weeping. His startling resemblance to his mother struck the old man forcefully.

"Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It's exactly like her, exactly like her, his mother. Spit some water on him, that's what I used to do for her. He's upset about his mother, his mother," he muttered to Ivan.

"But she was my mother too, I believe -- his mother. Wasn't she?" said Ivan, with unrestrained anger and contempt. The old man shrank back before his blazing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second; it seemed to have genuinely slipped the old man's mind that Alyosha's mother was Ivan's mother too.

"Your mother?" he muttered, not understanding. "What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind's never gone dark like that before. Forgive me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!" He stopped. A broad, drunken, half-senseless grin spread across his face.
At that moment a fearful noise and uproar came from the hall -- violent shouting, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man rushed to Ivan in terror.
"He'll kill me! He'll kill me! Don't let him near me!" he screamed, clutching at the skirt of Ivan's coat.

title: IX. The Sensualists
paragraphs: Grigory and Smerdyakov ran into the room right after Dmitri. They'd been struggling with him in the passage, trying to keep him out, following instructions Fyodor Pavlovitch had given them some days before. Taking advantage of the moment Dmitri paused to look around the room after entering, Grigory ran around the table, shut the double doors on the far side leading to the inner rooms, and planted himself in front of them, arms spread wide, ready to defend the entrance, as it were, with the last drop of his blood. Seeing this, Dmitri let out something more like a scream than a shout and lunged at Grigory.
"So she's there! She's hiding in there! Out of my way, you scoundrel!"

He tried to drag Grigory aside, but the old servant shoved him back. Beside himself with fury, Dmitri struck out and hit Grigory with all his strength. The old man dropped like a log, and Dmitri, leaping right over him, broke through the door. Smerdyakov stood pale and trembling at the far end of the room, pressed close against Fyodor Pavlovitch.
"She's here!" Dmitri shouted. "I saw her turn toward the house just now, but I couldn't catch her. Where is she? Where is she?"
That single cry, "She's here!" had an indescribable effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. Every trace of his terror vanished.

"Hold him! Hold him!" he cried, and dashed after Dmitri. Meanwhile Grigory had gotten up off the floor, but still seemed dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room, something fell to the floor with a ringing crash -- a large glass vase, not an expensive one, on a marble pedestal, which Dmitri had knocked over as he ran past.
"After him!" shouted the old man. "Help!"
Ivan and Alyosha caught the old man and forcibly hauled him back.
"Why are you running after him? He'll murder you outright," Ivan cried furiously at his father.
"Ivan! Alyosha! She has to be here. Grushenka's here. He said he saw her himself, running."
He was choking. He hadn't been expecting Grushenka at all, and the sudden news that she was here had made him beside himself. He was shaking all over. He seemed frantic.
"But you've seen for yourself that she hasn't come," cried Ivan.
"But she might have come in by that other entrance."
"You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key."

Dmitri suddenly reappeared in the drawing room. He had, of course, found the other entrance locked, and the key was indeed in Fyodor Pavlovitch's pocket. The windows of every room were shut too, so Grushenka couldn't have come in anywhere, and couldn't have run out anywhere either.

"Hold him!" shrieked Fyodor Pavlovitch, the moment he saw him again. "He's been stealing money out of my bedroom." And, tearing himself free of Ivan, he rushed at Dmitri again. But Dmitri threw up both hands and suddenly seized the old man by the two tufts of hair left on his temples, yanked at them, and flung him crashing to the floor. He kicked him two or three times in the face with his heel. The old man let out a shrill moan. Ivan, though not as strong as Dmitri, threw his arms around him and pulled him away with all his might. Alyosha helped too, with his slender strength, holding Dmitri back from the front.
"Madman! You've killed him!" cried Ivan.
"Serves him right!" shouted Dmitri, breathless. "If I haven't killed him, I'll come back and finish the job. You can't protect him forever!"
"Dmitri! Leave, right now!" Alyosha cried, commanding.
"Alexey! Tell me. You're the only one I can believe; was she here just now, or not? I saw her myself, creeping this way along the fence from the lane. I shouted, and she ran."
"I swear she hasn't been here, and no one was expecting her."

"But I saw her.... So she must... I'll find out right now where she is.... Goodbye, Alexey! Not a word to Aesop about the money now. But go to Katerina Ivanovna at once, and be sure to tell her: 'He sends his compliments to you!' His compliments, his compliments! Just compliments, and farewell! Describe the whole scene to her."

Meanwhile Ivan and Grigory had lifted the old man and settled him into an armchair. His face was covered in blood, but he was conscious, and listened greedily to Dmitri's shouting. He was still convinced that Grushenka really was somewhere in the house. Dmitri looked at him with hatred as he went out.
"I don't regret spilling your blood!" he cried. "Beware, old man, beware of your dream, because I have a dream of my own too. I curse you, and I disown you completely."
He ran out of the room.
"She's here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!" the old man wheezed, barely audible, beckoning with his finger.
"No, she's not here, you old lunatic!" Ivan shouted at him angrily. "Look, he's fainting! Water! A towel! Hurry, Smerdyakov!"

Smerdyakov ran for water. They finally got the old man undressed and put him to bed. They wrapped a wet towel around his head. Worn out from the brandy, the violent emotion, and the blows he'd taken, he closed his eyes and fell asleep the moment his head touched the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing room. Smerdyakov cleared away the pieces of the broken vase, while Grigory stood by the table, staring gloomily at the floor.
"Shouldn't you put a wet bandage on your own head and go to bed too?" Alyosha said to him. "We'll look after him. My brother gave you a terrible blow -- on the head."
"He's insulted me!" Grigory pronounced, gloomy and distinct.
"He's insulted his father, not just you," Ivan observed, with a forced smile.
"I used to wash him in his own tub. And he's insulted me," Grigory repeated.
"Damn it all, if I hadn't pulled him off, he might have killed him. It wouldn't take much to finish off Aesop, would it?" Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
"God forbid!" cried Alyosha.
"Why should he forbid it?" Ivan went on, still in a whisper, with a malicious twist to his mouth. "One reptile will devour the other. And serve them both right, too."
Alyosha shuddered.
"Of course I won't let him be murdered, any more than I did just now. Stay here, Alyosha, I'm going to take a turn in the yard. My head's started aching."

Alyosha went to his father's bedroom and sat beside the bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. The old man suddenly opened his eyes and stared at Alyosha for a long while, clearly remembering, clearly thinking things over. All at once his face showed extraordinary agitation.
"Alyosha," he whispered anxiously, "where's Ivan?"
"In the yard. He's got a headache. He's keeping watch."
"Give me that hand mirror. It's over there. Give it to me."

Alyosha handed him the little round folding mirror that stood on the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself in it; his nose was considerably swollen, and on the left side of his forehead there was a large crimson bruise.
"What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I'm afraid of Ivan. I'm more afraid of Ivan than of the other one. You're the only one I'm not afraid of...."
"Don't be afraid of Ivan either. He's angry, but he'll defend you."
"Alyosha, and what about the other one? He's run off to Grushenka. My angel, tell me the truth -- was she here just now, or not?"
"No one saw her. It was a mistake. She hasn't been here at all."
"You know Mitya wants to marry her -- marry her."
"She won't marry him."
"She won't. She won't. She won't. She won't, no matter what!"

The old man positively fluttered with joy, as though nothing more comforting could have been said to him. In his delight he seized Alyosha's hand and pressed it warmly to his heart. Tears actually glistened in his eyes.

"That image of the Mother of God I was telling you about just now," he said. "Take it home and keep it for yourself. And I'll let you go back to the monastery.... I was only joking this morning, don't be angry with me. My head hurts, Alyosha.... Alyosha, comfort my heart. Be an angel and tell me the truth!"
"You're still asking whether she's been here or not?" Alyosha asked, sorrowfully.

"No, no, no. I believe you. Here's what I want: you go to Grushenka yourself, or find some way to see her; hurry, ask her; find out for yourself which of us she means to choose, him or me. Eh? What? Can you do that?"
"If I see her, I'll ask her," Alyosha muttered, embarrassed.
"No, she won't tell you," the old man broke in. "She's a rogue. She'll start kissing you and say it's you she wants. She's a deceitful, shameless hussy. You mustn't go near her, you mustn't!"
"No, father, and it wouldn't be suitable anyway, it wouldn't be right at all."
"Where was he sending you just now? He shouted 'Go' as he ran off."
"To Katerina Ivanovna's."
"For money? To ask her for money?"
"No. Not for money."

"He hasn't got a farthing. I'll settle in for the night now, and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you'll run into her.... Only be sure to come to me tomorrow morning. Be sure to. I've got something to tell you tomorrow. Will you come?"
"Yes."
"When you come, pretend you've come of your own accord, just to ask how I am. Don't tell anyone I asked you to. Not a word to Ivan."
"Very well."
"Goodbye, my angel. You stood up for me just now. I'll never forget it. I've got something to tell you tomorrow -- but I have to think it over first."
"And how are you feeling now?"
"I'll get up tomorrow and go out, perfectly well, perfectly well!"

Crossing the yard, Alyosha found Ivan sitting on the bench by the gate. He was sitting there, writing something in pencil in his notebook. Alyosha told Ivan that their father had woken up, was conscious, and had sent him back to sleep at the monastery.
"Alyosha, I'd be very glad to meet you tomorrow morning," said Ivan cordially, standing up. His warmth caught Alyosha completely off guard.
"I'll be at the Hohlakovs' tomorrow," Alyosha answered, "and I may go to Katerina Ivanovna's too, if I don't manage to find her now."
"But you're going to see her now, anyway? For that 'compliments and farewell'?" Ivan said, smiling. Alyosha looked flustered.
"I think I understand his outburst just now, and part of what led up to it, well enough. Dmitri's asked you to go to her and tell her that he -- well, in short -- is taking his leave of her?"
"Brother, how will all this horror end, between father and Dmitri?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"There's no telling for certain. Maybe it'll come to nothing: it might all fizzle out. That woman's a beast. In any case, we have to keep the old man indoors and not let Dmitri into the house."
"Brother, let me ask you one more thing: does any man have the right to look at other men and decide who deserves to live?"
"Why bring worth into it at all? The matter's usually settled in men's hearts on much more ordinary grounds than that. And as for rights -- who doesn't have the right to wish for something?"
"Not for another man's death?"

"What if it were for another man's death? Why lie to ourselves, since everyone lives this way, and perhaps can't help living this way. Are you referring to what I said just now -- that one reptile will devour the other? In that case let me ask you: do you think I'm capable, like Dmitri, of spilling Aesop's blood -- of murdering him, eh?"
"What are you saying, Ivan? A thought like that never crossed my mind. I don't think Dmitri's capable of it either."

"Thanks, if only for that," Ivan smiled. "Rest assured, I'd always defend him. But when it comes to my own wishes, I reserve myself full latitude in this case. Goodbye till tomorrow. Don't condemn me, and don't think of me as a villain," he added, with a smile.
They shook hands warmly, as they'd never done before. Alyosha felt that his brother had taken the first step toward him, and that he'd certainly done it with some particular purpose in mind.

title: X. Both Together
paragraphs: Alyosha left his father's house feeling even more exhausted and downcast in spirit than when he'd entered it. His mind, too, felt shattered and unhinged, while he sensed he was afraid to piece together the disjointed fragments and form any general picture out of all the agonizing, conflicting experiences of the day. He felt something close to despair, which he'd never known before that day. Towering like a mountain over everything else stood the fatal, unanswerable question: how would things end between his father and his brother Dmitri, with this terrible woman between them? He'd now witnessed it himself, had been there, had seen them face to face. And yet it might only be his brother Dmitri who ended up unhappy, terribly, completely unhappy: trouble was waiting for him. It seemed, too, that other people were caught up in it, far more than Alyosha could have imagined before. There was something downright mysterious in it too. Ivan had taken a step toward him, which was exactly what Alyosha had long been hoping for. And yet now, for some reason, he felt frightened by it. And these women? Strange to say, that morning he'd set out for Katerina Ivanovna's in an agony of embarrassment; now he felt nothing of the kind. On the contrary, he was hurrying there as though expecting to find guidance from her. And yet delivering this message to her was obviously harder now than it had been before. The matter of the three thousand roubles was irrevocably settled, and Dmitri, feeling himself dishonored, his last hope gone, might sink to any depth. He had, besides, told him to describe to Katerina Ivanovna the scene that had just taken place with his father.

It was by now seven o'clock, and growing dark, as Alyosha entered the large, comfortable house on the High Street where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Alyosha knew she lived with two aunts. One of them, a woman of little education, was the aunt of her half sister Agafya Ivanovna, who had looked after her in her father's house when she came home from boarding school. The other aunt was a fashionable Moscow lady, though her circumstances were straitened. It was said that both of them deferred to Katerina Ivanovna in everything, and that she kept them with her only as chaperones. Katerina Ivanovna herself deferred to no one but her benefactress, the general's widow, who'd been confined to Moscow by illness, and to whom she was obliged to write twice a week, a full account of everything she did.

When Alyosha entered the hall and asked the maid who answered the door to announce him, it was clear they already knew he'd arrived. Perhaps he'd been noticed from the window. At any rate, Alyosha heard a commotion, caught the sound of hurrying footsteps and rustling skirts. Two or three women, perhaps, had just run out of the room.

Alyosha found it strange that his arrival should cause such a stir. He was shown into the drawing room at once, though. It was a large room, elegantly and lavishly furnished, nothing like the usual provincial style. There were sofas, couches, settees everywhere, big and small tables. There were paintings on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, masses of flowers, even an aquarium in the window. It was dusk, and rather dark. Alyosha made out a silk mantle thrown down on the sofa, where people had evidently just been sitting; and on a table in front of the sofa were two half-finished cups of chocolate, some cakes, a glass dish of blue raisins, and another of sweets. Alyosha saw he'd interrupted visitors, and frowned. But at that instant the curtain was drawn back, and Katerina Ivanovna came in with quick, hurrying steps, holding out both hands to Alyosha with a radiant, delighted smile. At the same moment a servant brought in two lit candles and set them on the table.
"Thank God! You've finally come too! I've been praying for you all day, simply praying! Sit down."

Alyosha had been struck by Katerina Ivanovna's beauty three weeks earlier, when Dmitri had first brought him, at her particular request, to be introduced to her. There had been no real conversation between them at that meeting, though. Assuming Alyosha was very shy, Katerina Ivanovna had talked the whole time to Dmitri, to spare him. Alyosha had stayed silent, but he'd seen a great deal, quite clearly. He'd been struck by the imperiousness, the proud ease, the self-assurance of the haughty girl. And he was certain of all that -- Alyosha felt he wasn't exaggerating it in the least. He thought her great glowing black eyes were very fine, especially set against her pale, rather sallow, longish face. But in those eyes, and in the line of her exquisite lips, there was something his brother might well fall passionately in love with, but which, perhaps, couldn't be loved for very long. He'd said almost exactly that to Dmitri afterward, when his brother pressed and insisted that he not hide his impressions of his betrothed.
"You'll be happy with her, but perhaps -- not peacefully happy."
"Quite right, brother. People like that never change. They don't bend to fate. So you think I won't love her forever."
"No -- perhaps you will love her forever. But perhaps you won't always be happy with her."

Alyosha had given his opinion at the time, blushing, and angry with himself for having given in to his brother's pleading and put such "foolish" ideas into words at all. His opinion had struck him as unbelievably foolish the moment he'd said it out loud. He'd felt ashamed, too, at having pronounced such a confident judgment about a woman. It was with all the more astonishment, then, that he now realized, at his very first glance at Katerina Ivanovna as she ran in to greet him, that he might have been utterly mistaken. This time her face glowed with spontaneous, good-natured warmth, with direct, wholehearted sincerity. The "pride and haughtiness" that had struck Alyosha so forcibly before showed itself now only as a frank, generous energy, and a kind of bright, powerful faith in herself. Alyosha understood at the first glance, at the very first word, that all the tragedy of her position with the man she loved so dearly was no secret to her; that she probably already knew everything, absolutely everything. And yet, in spite of that, there was such brightness in her face, such faith in the future. Alyosha felt at once that he'd badly wronged her in his thoughts. He was won over, captivated, immediately. Beyond all this, he noticed right away, from her very first words, that she was in a state of great excitement -- an excitement that seemed quite exceptional, almost bordering on ecstasy.
"I was so eager to see you, because you're the only one who can tell me the whole truth."
"I've come," Alyosha muttered, flustered, "I -- he sent me."

"Ah, he sent you! I knew he would. Now I know everything -- everything!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, her eyes flashing. "Wait a moment, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I'll tell you why I've been so desperate to see you. You see, I probably know a great deal more than you do yourself, and there's no need for you to tell me anything at all. I'll tell you what I want from you. I want to know your own last impression of him. I want you to tell me directly, plainly, even crudely if you have to -- oh, as crudely as you like -- what you thought of him just now, of his state of mind, after your meeting with him today. That would be better, maybe, than if I had it out with him in person, since he doesn't want to come to me. Do you understand what I'm asking of you? Now, tell me simply, tell me every word of the message he sent with you -- I knew he'd send you."
"He told me to give you his compliments -- and to say he'd never come again -- but to give you his compliments."
"His compliments? Was that the exact word he used?"
"Yes."
"Maybe he made a mistake in the word by accident, maybe he didn't use the right one?"
"No; he specifically told me to repeat that exact word. He begged me two or three times not to forget to say it."
Katerina Ivanovna flushed hotly.

"Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I really need your help now. I'll tell you what I think, and you just tell me whether it's right or not. Listen! If he'd sent me his compliments in passing, without insisting you repeat the exact words, without stressing them, that would be the end of everything! But if he particularly insisted on those exact words, if he particularly told you not to forget to repeat them to me -- then maybe he was in a state of excitement, beside himself. He'd made his decision and it frightened him. He wasn't walking away from me with a firm, steady step, he was leaping headlong. The emphasis on that phrase might have been nothing but bravado."
"Yes, yes!" Alyosha cried warmly. "I believe that's exactly it."
"And if that's so, he isn't altogether lost. I can still save him. Wait! Did he say anything to you about money -- about three thousand roubles?"

"He did mention it, and it's that, more than anything, that's crushing him. He said he'd lost his honor and that nothing matters now," Alyosha answered warmly, feeling a surge of hope in his heart, and beginning to believe there really might be some way out, some path to salvation for his brother. "But do you know about the money?" he added, and suddenly broke off.

"I've known about it for a long time; I telegraphed Moscow to ask, and learned long ago that the money never arrived. He never sent it, but I said nothing. Last week I found out he was still in need of money. My only aim in all of this was that he should know who to turn to, who his true friend was. No, he won't admit that I'm his truest friend; he won't know me, he only sees me as a woman. I've been tormented all week, trying to think how to keep him from feeling ashamed to face me over spending that three thousand. Let him be ashamed of himself, let him be ashamed that other people know -- but not that I know. He can tell God everything without shame. Why can't he understand how much I'm ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn't he know me? How dare he not know me, after everything that's happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he is, afraid he's dishonored in my eyes. Why -- he wasn't afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How is it I don't deserve the same?"
She spoke the last words in tears. Tears streamed from her eyes.
"I have to tell you," Alyosha began, his own voice trembling now, "what happened just now, between him and my father."

And he described the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how he'd broken in, knocked his father down, and afterward had again, urgently and specifically, begged him to deliver his compliments and farewell. "He went to that woman," Alyosha added, softly.
