"And do you suppose I can't put up with that woman? Does he think I can't? But he won't marry her," she suddenly laughed, a nervous laugh. "Could a passion like that really last forever, in a Karamazov? It's passion, not love. He won't marry her, because she won't marry him." Katerina Ivanovna laughed strangely again.
"He may marry her," Alyosha said mournfully, looking down.

"He won't marry her, I tell you. That girl's an angel. Do you know that? Do you know that?" Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed, suddenly, with extraordinary warmth. "She's one of the most fantastic of fantastic creatures alive. I know how bewitching she is, but I also know she's kind, firm, and noble. Why are you looking at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? Are you wondering at my words, maybe? You don't believe me? Agrafena Alexandrovna, my angel!" she suddenly cried out, peering into the next room, "come in to us. This is a friend. This is Alyosha. He knows everything about our affairs. Show yourself to him."
"I've just been waiting behind the curtain for you to call me," said a soft, one might even say sugary, feminine voice.

The curtain lifted and Grushenka herself came up to the table, smiling and beaming. A violent revulsion swept over Alyosha. He fixed his eyes on her and couldn't look away. Here she was, then, that awful woman, that "beast," as Ivan had called her half an hour before. And yet you'd have thought the creature standing in front of him the simplest, most ordinary woman alive -- good-natured, kind, handsome certainly, but so like plenty of other good-looking ordinary women! It's true she was very, very good-looking, with that particular Russian beauty so passionately loved by so many men. She was a fairly tall woman, though a little shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was exceptionally tall. She had a full figure, with soft, almost noiseless movements, her voice as softened, as oversweetened, as her step. She moved, not like Katerina Ivanovna, with a vigorous, confident stride, but noiselessly. Her feet made absolutely no sound on the floor. She sank softly into a low chair, her sumptuous black silk dress rustling softly, and settled her milk-white neck and broad shoulders delicately into an expensive cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two, and her face looked exactly that age. She was very fair-skinned, with a pale pink flush on her cheeks. Her face could be called somewhat too broad in its modeling, and her lower jaw jutted forward slightly. Her upper lip was thin, but the slightly protruding lower one was at least twice as full, and had a pouting look. But her magnificent, abundant dark brown hair, her sable eyebrows, and her charming gray-blue eyes with their long lashes would have made even the most indifferent passerby, meeting her by chance in a crowd on the street, stop and remember her face long afterward. What struck Alyosha most about that face was its expression of childlike good nature. There was something childlike in her eyes, a look of childish delight. She came up to the table, glowing with delight, as though expecting something, with a childish, impatient, trusting curiosity. The light in her eyes gladdened the soul -- Alyosha felt that at once. There was something else about her, too, that he couldn't quite grasp or put a name to, and which nevertheless, perhaps unconsciously, affected him all the same. It was a certain softness, a voluptuousness to her physical movements, a catlike noiselessness. And yet it was a vigorous, ample body underneath. Beneath the shawl one could make out full, broad shoulders, a high, still girlish bosom. Her figure suggested the lines of the Venus de Milo, though already somewhat exaggerated in proportion. That much could be told already. Connoisseurs of Russian beauty could have predicted, with real confidence, that this fresh, still-youthful beauty would lose its harmony by the time she was thirty, would "spread"; that the face would grow puffy, that wrinkles would appear before long on the forehead and around the eyes; that the complexion would coarsen, might even redden -- in short, that this was the beauty of a moment, the fleeting beauty so often found among Russian women. Alyosha, of course, wasn't thinking any of this; but fascinated as he was, he still felt an unpleasant twinge, a kind of regret, wondering why she drawled her words that way and couldn't speak naturally. She did it, clearly, because she felt there was some charm in the exaggerated, honeyed way she drew out her syllables. It was, of course, nothing but a bad, underbred habit, betraying poor upbringing and a false notion of good manners. And yet this way of talking struck Alyosha as almost unbelievably at odds with the childishly simple, happy expression on her face, the soft, babyish joy in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna sat her down at once in an armchair facing Alyosha, and kissed her rapturously, again and again, on her smiling lips. She seemed positively in love with her.

"This is the first time we've met, Alexey Fyodorovitch," she said, rapturously. "I wanted to know her, to see her. I wanted to go to her, and no sooner had I said so than she came to me. I knew we'd settle everything together -- everything. My heart told me so -- people begged me not to take this step, but I could tell it would be the way out of the whole difficulty, and I wasn't wrong. Grushenka's explained everything to me, told me everything she intends to do. She flew here like an angel of goodness, and brought us peace and joy."
"You didn't disdain me, sweet, excellent young lady," Grushenka drawled, in her singsong voice, still with that same charming, delighted smile.

"Don't you dare talk to me like that, you sorceress, you witch! Disdain you! Here, I have to kiss that lower lip of yours again. It looks like it's swelling, and now it'll swell even more, more and more. Look how she laughs, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It does the heart good just to look at the angel."
Alyosha flushed, and faint, barely perceptible shivers kept running through him.
"You make far too much of me, dear young lady, and maybe I'm not worthy of your kindness at all."

"Not worthy! She says she's not worthy of it!" Katerina Ivanovna cried again, with the same warmth. "You know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we're fanciful, we're willful, but the proudest of the proud, deep in our little heart. We're noble, we're generous, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let me tell you that. We've only ever been unfortunate. We were too ready to sacrifice everything for a man who was, perhaps, unworthy of it, or fickle. There was a man once -- one, an officer too -- we loved him, we sacrificed everything for him. That was long ago, five years back, and he's forgotten us, he's married since. Now he's a widower, he's written to say he's coming, and, do you know, we've loved him, only him, this whole time, and we'll love him our whole lives! He'll come, and Grushenka will be happy again. For the last five years she's been wretched. But who can blame her for that, who can hold her past against her? Only that bedridden old merchant, and he's more like a father to her, a friend, a protector. He found her back then, in despair, in agony, abandoned by the man she loved. She was ready to drown herself then, but the old merchant saved her -- saved her!"
"You're being very kind to defend me, dear young lady. You're in a great hurry about everything," Grushenka drawled again.

"Defend you! Is it for me to defend you? Should I even dare to defend you? Grushenka, angel, give me your hand. Look at that charming, soft little hand, Alexey Fyodorovitch! Look at it! It's brought me happiness, it's lifted me up, and I'm going to kiss it, outside and in, here, here, here!"

And three times, in a kind of rapture, she kissed Grushenka's hand -- charming, certainly, though rather plump. Grushenka held it out with a musical, charming little nervous laugh, watching the "sweet young lady," plainly enjoying having her hand kissed.
"Maybe there's a bit too much rapture in all this," thought Alyosha. He blushed. He'd felt a peculiar unease in his heart the whole time.
"You won't make me blush, dear young lady, kissing my hand like that in front of Alexey Fyodorovitch."
"Do you think I meant to make you blush?" said Katerina Ivanovna, a little surprised. "Ah, my dear, how little you understand me!"

"Well, maybe you don't understand me either, dear young lady. Maybe I'm not as good as I seem to you. I've got a bad heart; I'll always have my own way. I charmed poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day simply for the fun of it."
"But now you'll save him. You've given me your word. You'll explain everything to him. You'll tell him you've long loved another man, who's now offering you his hand."
"Oh, no! I never gave you my word to do any such thing. It was you who kept talking about all that. I never gave you my word."
"Then I misunderstood you," Katerina Ivanovna said slowly, going a little pale. "You promised --"

"Oh, no, angel lady, I never promised anything," Grushenka interrupted, soft and even, still with that same gay, simple expression. "You see at once, dear young lady, what a willful wretch I am, next to you. If I want to do a thing, I do it. I might have promised you something just now. But now I'm thinking again: maybe I'll go back to Mitya after all. I liked him a great deal once -- liked him for almost a whole hour. Maybe I'll go now and tell him to stay with me from this day on. You see how changeable I am."
"Just now you said -- something quite different," Katerina Ivanovna whispered, faintly.
"Ah, just now! But you know, I'm such a soft-hearted, silly creature. Just think what he's gone through, on my account! What if, when I get home, I feel sorry for him? What then?"
"I never expected --"

"Ah, young lady, how good and generous you are, compared to me! Maybe now you won't care for a silly creature like me, now that you know what I'm really like. Give me your sweet little hand, angel lady," she said tenderly, and took Katerina Ivanovna's hand with something like reverence.

"Here, dear young lady, I'll take your hand and kiss it, the way you kissed mine. You kissed mine three times, but I ought to kiss yours three hundred to be even with you. Well, let that be. And then it'll be as God wills. Maybe I'll end up your slave entirely, wanting to do your bidding like a slave. Let it be as God wills, without any agreements or promises. What a sweet hand -- what a sweet hand you have! You sweet young lady, you unbelievable beauty!"
She slowly raised the hand to her lips, with what really did seem the odd aim of "getting even" with her in kisses.

Katerina Ivanovna didn't pull her hand away. She listened with a timid hope to these last words, though Grushenka's promise to do her bidding like a slave was strangely put. She looked intently into her eyes; she still saw in them the same simple-hearted, trusting expression, the same bright cheerfulness.
"She's perhaps too naive," thought Katerina Ivanovna, with a flicker of hope.

Grushenka, meanwhile, seemed positively enthralled by the "sweet hand." She raised it deliberately to her lips. But she held it there, near her mouth, for two or three minutes, as though reconsidering something.
"Do you know, angel lady," she suddenly drawled, her voice even softer and more sugary than before, "do you know, after all, I don't think I'll kiss your hand?" And she gave a little merry laugh.
"As you please. What's the matter with you?" said Katerina Ivanovna, starting suddenly.
"So that you'll have something to remember -- that you kissed my hand, but I didn't kiss yours."
There was a sudden gleam in her eyes. She looked at Katerina Ivanovna with a terrible intensity.
"Insolent creature!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, as though suddenly grasping something. She flushed all over and leapt up from her seat.
Grushenka got up too, but without any hurry.
"So I'll tell Mitya how you kissed my hand, but I didn't kiss yours at all. And how he'll laugh!"
"Vile slut! Get out!"
"Ah, for shame, young lady! Ah, for shame! That's not becoming of you at all, dear young lady, a word like that."
"Get out! You're a woman for sale!" screamed Katerina Ivanovna. Every feature of her face was twisted, utterly distorted.
"For sale, indeed! You used to visit gentlemen after dark for money once, didn't you -- putting your beauty up for sale. You see, I know all about it."
Katerina Ivanovna shrieked, and would have flown at her, but Alyosha held her back with all his strength.
"Not one step, not a word! Don't speak, don't answer her. She'll go -- she'll go this instant."
At that same moment Katerina Ivanovna's two aunts ran in at her cry, along with a maidservant. Everyone rushed to her side.
"I'll go," said Grushenka, taking her mantle up from the sofa. "Alyosha, darling, see me home!"
"Go away -- go away, hurry!" cried Alyosha, clasping his hands, pleading.
"Dear little Alyosha, see me home! I've got a lovely little story to tell you on the way. I put on this whole scene for your benefit, Alyosha. See me home, dear, you'll be glad of it afterward."
Alyosha turned away, wringing his hands. Grushenka ran out of the house, laughing musically.
Katerina Ivanovna fell into hysterics. She sobbed, shaken with convulsions. Everyone fussed around her.

"I warned you," said the elder of her two aunts. "I tried to stop you doing this. You're too impulsive. How could you do such a thing? You don't know creatures like that, and they say she's worse than any of them. You're much too willful."
"She's a tigress!" Katerina Ivanovna shrieked. "Why did you hold me back, Alexey Fyodorovitch? I'd have beaten her -- beaten her!"
She couldn't control herself in front of Alyosha; perhaps, indeed, she didn't even try to.
"She ought to be whipped in public, on a scaffold!"
Alyosha edged back toward the door.

"But, my God!" cried Katerina Ivanovna, clasping her hands. "He! He! How could he be so dishonorable, so inhuman! Why, he told that creature what happened on that terrible, cursed day! 'You brought your beauty for sale, dear young lady.' She knows it! Your brother's a scoundrel, Alexey Fyodorovitch."
Alyosha wanted to say something, but couldn't find the words. His heart ached.
"Go, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It's shameful, it's dreadful for me! Come tomorrow, I beg you, on my knees, come tomorrow. Don't judge me. Forgive me. I don't know what I'm going to do with myself now!"
Alyosha walked out into the street reeling. He could have wept, just as she had. Suddenly the maid caught up with him.
"The young lady forgot to give you this letter from Madame Hohlakov; it's been here since dinnertime."
Alyosha took the little pink envelope mechanically and, almost without noticing, put it in his pocket.

title: XI. Another Reputation Ruined
paragraphs: It wasn't much more than three-quarters of a mile from town to the monastery. Alyosha walked quickly along the road, deserted at that hour. It was almost night now, too dark to make anything out clearly thirty paces ahead. There was a crossroads halfway there. A figure appeared under a solitary willow at the crossroads. The moment Alyosha reached it, the figure stepped out and rushed at him, shouting savagely:
"Your money or your life!"
"So it's you, Mitya," Alyosha cried, startled, genuinely shaken despite his surprise.

"Ha ha ha! You didn't expect me? I couldn't decide where to wait for you. By her house? There are three roads from there, and I might have missed you. Finally I thought of waiting here, since you had to pass this way -- there's no other road to the monastery. Come on, tell me the truth. Crush me like a beetle. But what's wrong?"

"Nothing, brother -- it's just the fright you gave me. Oh, Dmitri! Father's blood, just now." (Alyosha started to cry; he'd been on the verge of tears for a while now, and something seemed to snap inside him at last.) "You nearly killed him -- cursed him -- and now -- here you are -- cracking jokes -- 'Your money or your life!'"
"Well, what of it? It's not proper -- is that it? Not suitable, given my situation?"
"No -- I only --"

"Wait. Look at the night. Look how dark it is, what clouds, what a wind's come up. I hid here under the willow, waiting for you. And, as God's my witness, I suddenly thought, why keep on suffering, what's there left to wait for? Here's a willow, a handkerchief, a shirt -- I could twist them into a rope in a minute, and braces besides, and why go on burdening the earth, dishonoring it with my vile presence? And then I heard you coming -- Heavens, it was as though something flew down and struck me right then. So there is a man, after all, whom I love. Here he is, that man, my dear little brother, whom I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the whole world. And I loved you so much, so much, right at that moment, that I thought, 'I'll throw myself on his neck this instant.' Then a stupid idea struck me, to play a joke on you, give you a scare. I shouted like a fool, 'Your money!' Forgive my foolishness -- it was just nonsense, and there's nothing unseemly in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Strike me, crush me, don't spare me! Was she furious?"
"No, not that.... There was nothing like that, Mitya. There -- I found them both there."
"Both? Who?"
"Grushenka, at Katerina Ivanovna's."
Dmitri was struck dumb.
"Impossible!" he cried. "You're raving! Grushenka, with her?"

Alyosha described everything that had happened from the moment he'd gone in to see Katerina Ivanovna. It took him about ten minutes to tell the whole story. He couldn't exactly be said to have told it smoothly or in order, but he seemed to make it clear enough, leaving out no word or gesture of any importance, and vividly describing, often in a single word, his own feelings as they happened. Dmitri listened in silence, staring at him with a terrible, fixed gaze, but it was clear to Alyosha that he understood it all, had grasped every point. But as the story went on, his face grew not just gloomy but menacing. He scowled, clenched his teeth, and his fixed stare grew even more rigid, more concentrated, more terrible -- when suddenly, with astonishing speed, his wrathful, savage expression changed, his tightly compressed lips parted, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch broke into helpless, spontaneous laughter. He literally shook with it. For a long time he couldn't speak.

"So she wouldn't kiss her hand! So she didn't kiss it -- so she ran off!" he kept exclaiming, with a kind of hysterical delight -- insolent delight, you might even call it, if it hadn't been so completely genuine. "So the other one called her a tigress! And a tigress she is! So she ought to be flogged on a scaffold? Yes, yes, exactly what I think; she ought to have been, long ago. It's like this, brother -- let her be punished, but I have to get better first. I understand her, that queen of insolence. That's her all over! You saw the whole of her in that hand-kissing business, the she-devil! She's magnificent, in her own way! So she ran home? I'll go -- ah -- I'll run to her! Alyosha, don't blame me, I agree that hanging's too good for her."
"But Katerina Ivanovna!" Alyosha exclaimed, sorrowfully.

"I see her too! I see right through her, like never before! It's practically a discovery of the four continents of the world -- or five, rather! What a thing to do! That's just like Katya, wasn't it, not afraid to face down a coarse, ill-mannered officer, risking a deadly insult, out of pure generosity, to save her father! But the pride, the recklessness, the sheer defiance of fate, the unbounded defiance of it! You say that aunt tried to stop her? That aunt, you know, is overbearing in her own right. She's the sister of the general's widow in Moscow, and even more high and mighty than she is. But her husband was caught stealing government money. He lost everything -- his estate, all of it -- and the proud wife had to lower her colors, and hasn't raised them since. So she tried to stop Katya, but Katya wouldn't listen to her! She thinks she can overcome anything, that everything will bend to her will. She thought she could bewitch Grushenka if she wanted to, and she believed it herself -- she's playing a part for her own benefit, and whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka's hand first on purpose, with some scheme in mind? No, she really was captivated by Grushenka -- or rather, not by Grushenka, but by her own dream, her own delusion -- because it was her dream, her delusion! Alyosha, darling, how did you get away from those women, from the pair of them? Did you hitch up your cassock and run? Ha ha ha!"

"Brother, you don't seem to have noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna, telling Grushenka about that day. And she flung it right back in her face just now -- that she'd gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what could be worse than that insult?"
What troubled Alyosha more than anything was that, incredible as it seemed, his brother appeared actually pleased by Katerina Ivanovna's humiliation.

"Bah!" Dmitri scowled fiercely and struck his forehead with his hand. He was only just realizing it now, though Alyosha had already told him of the insult, and of Katerina Ivanovna's cry: "Your brother's a scoundrel!"

"Yes, maybe I really did tell Grushenka about that 'fatal day,' as Katya calls it. Yes, I did tell her, I remember! It was that time at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, kneeling and praying before Katya's image, and Grushenka understood it. She understood everything, even then. I remember -- she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it was bound to end this way, all the same.... Then she cried, but now it's 'the dagger in the heart'! That's how women are."
He looked down and sank into thought.

"Yes, I'm a scoundrel, a thorough scoundrel!" he said suddenly, gloomily. "It doesn't matter whether I cried or not, I'm still a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the name, if that's any comfort to her. Come, that's enough. Goodbye. There's no point talking about it! It's not amusing. You go your way, and I'll go mine. And I don't want to see you again, except as a last resort. Goodbye, Alexey!"
He pressed Alyosha's hand warmly, and, still looking down, without raising his head, as though tearing himself away, turned quickly back toward town.
Alyosha watched him go, unable to believe he'd leave so abruptly.

"Wait, Alexey, one more confession, to you alone!" Dmitri suddenly cried, turning back. "Look at me. Look at me carefully. You see here, here -- there's terrible disgrace in store for me." (As he said "here," Dmitri struck his chest with his fist, in a strange way, as though the dishonor lay precisely at that spot, on his chest, in a pocket, perhaps, or hung round his neck.) "You know me now, a scoundrel, an open scoundrel, but let me tell you that I've never done anything before, and never will again, that could compare in baseness with the dishonor I'm carrying right now, at this very minute, on my chest, here, here -- which is going to happen, even though I'm perfectly free to stop it. I can stop it, or carry it through -- mark that. Well, let me tell you, I'm going to carry it through. I won't stop it. I told you everything just now, but I didn't tell you this, because even I didn't have the nerve for it. I could still pull back; if I do, I could give back the full half of my lost honor tomorrow. But I won't pull back. I'll carry out my vile plan, and you can bear witness that I told you so beforehand. Darkness and ruin! No need to explain further. You'll find out in due time. The filthy back alley, and the she-devil. Goodbye. Don't pray for me, I'm not worth it. And there's no need, no need at all.... I don't need it! Away!"
And he suddenly pulled away, this time for good. Alyosha went on toward the monastery.
"What? I'll never see him again! What does he mean?" he wondered wildly. "Why, I'll certainly see him tomorrow. I'll go look for him. I'll make a point of it. What did he mean?"

He walked around the monastery and crossed the pine wood to the hermitage. The door was opened to him, though no one was normally admitted at that hour. There was a tremor in his heart as he stepped into Father Zossima's cell.

"Why, why had he sent him out into the world? Why had he sent him forth? Here was peace. Here was holiness. But out there was confusion, darkness in which a man lost his way and went astray at once...."

In the cell he found the novice Porfiry, along with Father Païssy, who came every hour to check on Father Zossima. Alyosha learned, with alarm, that he was growing steadily worse. Even the elder's usual talk with the brothers couldn't take place that day. As a rule, every evening after the service, the monks would gather in Father Zossima's cell, and all would confess their sins of the day aloud, their sinful thoughts and temptations, even any quarrels they'd had. Some confessed on their knees. The elder absolved them, reconciled them, counseled, imposed penance, blessed, and dismissed them. It was against this general "confession" that the opponents of the eldership protested, insisting it was a profanation of the sacrament of confession, close to sacrilege, though this was really something quite different. They'd even reported to the diocesan authorities that such confessions accomplished no real good, but actually led, to a considerable degree, to sin and temptation. Many of the brothers disliked going to the elder, and went only against their own will, since everyone went, and out of fear they'd be accused of pride and rebellious thinking. It was said some of the monks agreed among themselves beforehand: "I'll confess I lost my temper with you this morning, and you back me up on it," just so as to have something to say. Alyosha knew this actually happened sometimes. He also knew that some among the monks deeply resented the fact that letters from relatives were routinely brought to the elder first, to be opened and read by him before they reached the people they were addressed to.

It was assumed, of course, that all this was done freely, in good faith, as an act of voluntary submission and beneficial guidance. But, in truth, there was often no small amount of insincerity in it, a good deal that was false and strained in the practice. And yet the older, more experienced monks held to their view, arguing that "for those who've come within these walls sincerely seeking salvation, this kind of obedience and sacrifice will certainly prove beneficial, of real value; while those who find it irksome, and grumble against it, aren't true monks at all, and made a mistake ever entering the monastery -- their proper place is out in the world. Even inside the temple, no one's safe from sin and the devil. So there's no point dwelling on it too much."

"He's weaker, a drowsiness has come over him," Father Païssy whispered to Alyosha, as he blessed him. "It's hard to rouse him. And he mustn't be roused. He woke for five minutes, sent his blessing to the brothers, and asked for their prayers for him tonight. He means to take the sacrament again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked whether you'd gone away, and was told you were in town. 'I blessed him for that work,' he said, 'his place is there, not here, for a while.' Those were his exact words about you. He remembered you with love, with anxiety; do you understand how highly he honors you? But how has he decided that you should spend some time out in the world? He must have foreseen something in your fate! Understand, Alexey, that if you go back into the world, it must be to do the duty laid on you by your elder, and not for frivolous vanity or worldly pleasures."

Father Païssy went out. Alyosha had no doubt now that Father Zossima was dying, though he might live another day or two yet. Alyosha resolved firmly and fervently that, in spite of all his promises to his father, the Hohlakovs, and Katerina Ivanovna, he wouldn't leave the monastery the next day, but would stay with his elder to the end. His heart glowed with love, and he reproached himself bitterly for having been able, even for one instant, to forget the man he'd left in the monastery on his deathbed, the man he honored above anyone else in the world. He went into Father Zossima's bedroom, knelt down, and bowed to the ground before the elder, who slept quietly, without stirring, his breathing regular, barely audible, his face peaceful.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had received his guests that morning. Taking off his boots, he lay down on the hard, narrow leather sofa he'd long used as a bed, bringing nothing but a pillow. He'd long since forgotten about the mattress his father had shouted about that morning. He took off his cassock and used it as a blanket. But before going to sleep, he knelt and prayed for a long time. In his fervent prayer he didn't ask God to lighten his darkness, but only thirsted for that joyful emotion which always came over his soul after praise and adoration, the way his evening prayers usually ended. That joy always brought him a light, untroubled sleep. As he was praying, he suddenly felt, in his pocket, the little pink note the servant had handed him as he left Katerina Ivanovna's. He was disturbed by it, but finished his prayer first. Then, after some hesitation, he opened the envelope. Inside was a letter addressed to him, signed by Lise, the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov, who had laughed at him in front of the elder that very morning.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch," she wrote, "I'm writing to you without anyone knowing, even mamma, and I know how wrong that is. But I can't go on living without telling you what's sprung up in my heart, and for now no one but the two of us must know it. But how am I supposed to say what I want so badly to tell you? Paper, they say, doesn't blush, but I promise you that's not true, and that it's blushing right now, just like I am, all over. Dear Alyosha, I love you, I've loved you since I was a child, since our Moscow days, when you were very different from how you are now, and I'll love you my whole life. My heart has chosen you, to join our lives together and carry them on to old age. Of course, on the condition that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we'll wait for whatever the law requires. By then I'll certainly be quite strong, I'll be walking and dancing. There's no doubt about that."

"You see how I've thought of everything. There's only one thing I can't picture: what you'll think of me when you read this. I'm always laughing and being naughty. I made you angry this morning, but I promise you, before I even picked up my pen, I prayed before the Image of the Mother of God, and I'm praying now, and I'm almost crying."

"My secret's in your hands now. When you come tomorrow, I don't know how I'll be able to look at you. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, what if I can't hold myself back, like a silly thing, and laugh when I look at you, the way I did today? You'll think I'm a nasty girl making fun of you, and you won't believe my letter at all. And so I beg you, dear one, if you have any pity for me at all, when you come tomorrow, don't look me straight in the face, because if I meet your eyes, it's sure to make me laugh, especially since you'll be wearing that long robe. I go cold all over just thinking about it, so when you come, don't look at me at all for a while, look at mamma, or out the window...."

"So there, I've written you a love letter. Oh dear, what have I done? Alyosha, don't despise me, and if I've done something truly awful and hurt you, forgive me. Now the secret of my reputation, ruined forever perhaps, is in your hands."
"I'm certainly going to cry today. Goodbye until we meet, our awful meeting. -- LISE.
"P.S. -- Alyosha! You must, must, must come! -- LISE."

Alyosha read the note in amazement, read it through twice, thought for a moment, and suddenly let out a soft, sweet laugh. He caught himself. That laugh struck him as sinful, somehow. But a minute later he laughed again, just as softly, just as happily. He slowly folded the note back into its envelope, crossed himself, and lay down. The turmoil in his heart passed at once. "God, have mercy on all of them, keep all these unhappy, restless souls in your care, and set them on the right path. All roads are yours. Save them according to your wisdom. You are love. You will send joy to all!" Alyosha murmured, crossing himself, and drifted into peaceful sleep.
